maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In this and other debates that have taken place during the present session, Mr. Speaker, a good many things have been said about the high prices of necessities and the cost of living. Some things have also been mentioned about profiteering. I should like again to record our views in this respect. Although we have already expressed our regrets that in its present program-that is, the program to meet the present emergency -the government has not included some provision or some mechanism for checking the rising cost of living, I think I should mention again in this debate one or two things which we think are extremely important in con-, nection with this rather serious matter.
Following up what I mentioned this morning about candy bars and things of that sort, may I say that I think the people of Canada could do a good deal for themselves in controlling the cost of living if, 'wherever they see evidences of profiteering or of prices out of line, they just would not buy the stuff. I have never heard of a business that could carry on for any great length of time without customers. While I am not suggesting a boycott of any particular commodity, I suggest this. If the Canadian people [DOT]as a whole would not be so foolish as to pay the prices that are asked, I am satisfied that in many

cases a salutary lesson would be taught and the cost of living would perhaps be adjusted downward.
We have a four-point program for dealing with the situation at the present time without the imposition of over-all controls. I followed what the minister said, and it seemed to me that his arguments were fairly sound, particularly in relation to a time such as that in which we are now living. Our first point is this. We believe that the compensated price discount mechanism-that is, the subsidy method-could be used with good results, especially if we were to select some of those things that are most frequently bought and1 used by the people. We feel that the effect would be to bring about a general lowering of the cost of living if such" a mechanism were to be applied to even a moderate number of things. As was pointed out in this debate before the lunch hour, the cost would certainly be small having regard to the widespread good that would be done.
The second point that we suggest is this. If we couple with the compensated price discount mechanism early government action to correct the faults in our trade policy and to bring our trade nearer into balance, we feel that much could be done to assist in a general lowering of the cost of living. It must appeal to anyone's mind that as long as we persist in a favourable-trade-balance policy, that of sending out more goods and services than we bring back into Canada, we are inevitably going to push up the cost of living by making goods somewhat scarce. For example, the various government bureaux report a favourable trade balance in 1949 of something over $260 million. As can be seen, that policy contributes on the one hand to a shortage of goods, in that it drains off an unusually large percentage of our best Canadian production. In peacetime especially that large proportion of our best Canadian production, of such things as lumber, beef, and so on, going out chasing after scarce American dollars, has that effect. Then at the same time, when we do not bring back goods in payment for our exports, we have of course contributed to the scarcity. We find such hon. members as the hon. member for Greenwood' (Mr. Macdonnell) stating that the real cause is an inflation of currency, when as a matter of fact it is a part of our trade policy that is at fault and that is contributing to this whole condition of inflation or high cost of living.
Before I leave that second point may I say this. If we were to bring our trade more into balance so that when we send exports out of this country we are prepared to bring back imports in full payment for them, we would have less difficulty in controlling the cost of 69262-39J
The Budget-Mr. Low living. We feel that the government has not taken full advantage of the opportunities that have presented themselves during these past few years to balance our trade, or at least to bring it more nearly into balance, and that therefore to a degree they are responsible for the measure of inflation we may have as a result of sending out more goods than we bring back.
I now come to our third point. It seems to me that the government should investigate most carefully the whole taxation structure in order to discover what effects the various taxes have on production and on prices. To follow up their investigation, it seems to me that those taxes which prove to have inflated prices should be abolished or at least modified in the interests of lowering the cost of living.
A fourth important point in the program would be this. Along with the minister who expressed himself so well in his budget address, we think that the government should proceed to remove every discouragement to all-out production and to offer every encouragement in order to see to it that Canadian production of all kinds of wanted goods and services is kept at the highest possible level. We need a commission similar to the one that was appointed by President Hoover in the United States in 1934,-and we have already made that suggestion-one which at one and the same time investigates the potential productive capacity of Canada and the reasons why the national income does not at any time equal the gross national production. When we have discovered these things it seems to me that the minister will be in a far better position to determine what the tax base is going to be in the years to come when he actually needs to get back the tremendous quantities of revenue to meet whatever the world situation may bring, in addition to continuing the services that Canadians desire. So we advocate most strongly a commission to discover our potential productive capacity, and along with it an investigation commission to look into the question of governmental economy.
The other day I was pleased to hear the minister, in giving his budget address, admit that there were places where the government could effect economy. I am satisfied that sometimes the ministers themselves get too near to the thing to be able to see clearly, and it would therefore be advisable to have someone who is not quite so closely associated with the whole business of government to make an investigation and report on economies that might be effected in government.

The Budget-Mr. Low
I am not going to say at this time, Mr. Speaker, that I know there are gross overexpenditures, but certainly everyone knows, from his ordinary observation, that there are places where the government could effect economies in order to prevent the necessity for such large expenditures on the ordinary services of the country.
We realize that adjustments must be made in our economy in times like these. It is quite clear to us that much of the adjustment must come from the field of finance. Certainly we have to be realistic in dealing with the factors that contribute to the inflation that has been mentioned so often. Perhaps no financial project is of more importance to the people-no more important one could be undertaken by the government- than one which would stabilize the value of the Canadian dollar. In general when there is more money than goods it becomes necessary to draw off the excess of purchasing power through taxation or the sale of bonds -preferably, in our way of thinking, tax bonds.
When there is a deficiency of purchasing power we advocate the use of government machinery to create and inject into the bloodstream of our country just enough new money to keep the value of the dollar stable. The value of the dollar has been allowed to deteriorate rather dangerously, and it is because of that deterioration in its value that so many people, such as those with fixed incomes, are now suffering; their fixed incomes do not in any way match the prices that they have to pay for their necessities.
While I am speaking of the money supply, Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should place on record some interesting facts. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) very often has had things to say about the Canadian money supply. He had often indicated that the government should have long ago applied a policy of deflation to readjust our economy downwards. I heard him talk about that at considerable length this morning, and on other occasions he has done so. In this debate the hon. member has referred to the budget speech which was made by the former minister of finance, Mr. Ilsley, on September [DOT]12, 1939. At that time we were facing the necessity of making a real war effort. I have heard the hon. member, as well as the Minister of Finance, say that this budget speech of Mr. Ilsley was a classic of its kind. I want to quote two brief extracts from that speech, and I refer to those parts which are found on page 138 of Hansard for Tuesday, September 12, 1939.


In the first quotation Mr. Ilsley had been outlining the various ways in which the government could obtain revenues to make an all-out war effort, and this is what he said:
We can also divert our resources to war purposes by inflation. We can create additional supplies of money and use them to purchase what we need. In this case, just as in the others, what we take for war purposes someone else must do without. Instead of taking money from the individual citizen in the form of taxes or loans, we put our new money into competition with this old money and take the goods and services away from him by forcing prices up against him.
Further on he said:
All this is not to say that a small and carefully regulated amount of credit expansion may not be desirable in the early stages of the war in order to assist the increase of production and employment. It must be small and carefully controlled because its effects which may not appear immediately are cumulative and otherwise might get out of hand.	.
That ends the quotation I wanted to read, but you will note, Mr. Speaker, that Mr. Ilsley is very cautious about the use of what he is pleased to term the mechanism of inflation-that is, the creation by government of purchasing power and spending it into existence or into circulation to purchase what the government would need at the time, particularly for war purposes.
It is a fact that in 1939 the government did create and spend into circulation for the war effort, to get it started and to stimulate allout production and so on, about $200 million. That was not borrowed, and therefore no interest had to be paid on it.
I think it would be interesting to hon. members to find out just how far Canada has gone in this matter of expanding of credits, which Mr. Ilsley stated in 1939 would have to be handled very carefully; and the amount, he said, must be very small; we must discontinue expanding credits as soon as we get the machines of our economy turning again and employment figures going up. The facts and the figures that I am going to put in the record now are certainly not in accord with the opinion of Mr. Ilsley, as expressed by him in the speech from which I have already quoted.
Just how far Canada has gone in the matter of credit expansion since that speech was made? The best evidence that I have been able to find lies in the Bank of Canada's statements and reports, and I hold in my hand the one for May of 1950, from which I gathered these most interesting figures.
In 1939 the total of deposits in the chartered banks of Canada stood at $2,914 million. In April, 1950, the total money supply -that is, the total money deposits in the banks of Canada-stood at $8,137 million. There is indicated there an increase of

$5,223 million. We can account for this tremendous expansion that has taken place since 1939 in the following ways. First, the chartered banks purchased bonds with the expansion of credit, which has been done to a considerable degree by merely making available to the government new purchasing power after the government has deposited with them their bonds, on which the government pays the banks interest; second, by loans to government on treasury bills as security; third, through loans to producers through the expansion of credit, and fourth, through the accumulation of comparatively small amounts of foreign deposits.
Perhaps one of the best ways to show what has taken place in Canada since 1939 by way of currency and credit expansion is by quoting from this same Bank of Canada report for May, 1950, and particularly from a statement showing the total of general public holdings of certain liquid assets as they are set out at page 75 of that report. These liquid assets include currency, both notes and coin; active bank deposits; inactive bank deposits, and government of Canada securities-bonds and treasury bills.
On December 31, 1938, not long before the war broke out, the total of these forms of liquid assets was $5,788 million, which by 1950 had grown to $18,077 million. Those securities or those forms of liquid assets were not just picked up from the scrap heap; they were created during that period of time and showed an increase between 1938 and 1950 of $12,289 million.
This tremendous increase can be accounted for only by the action of the governments and banks of the country in creating new purchasing power. That is the only way in which it can be done. As I said, between 1938 and 1950, $12,289 million in new purchasing power had been created jointly by the governments and the banks'-the chartered banks of the country. I am not suggesting by any means that this could have been accomplished without the co-operation of the producers. Of course the producers got to work and made use of the loans they obtained to produce goods and services, and thereby helped to back the credit and currency which were expanded.
The $12,289 million expansion since 1939 it seems to me makes Mr. Ilsley's statement of September 12, 1939, look rather like the statement of one who is activated by fear rather than by knowledge. On page 140 of Hansard of September 12, 1939, Mr. Ilsley said:
However, as soon as the expansion of employment and production gets well under way and certainly
The Budget-Mr. Low
before it approaches its limits, further expansion of the supply of money and credit must be stopped if the danger of progressive inflation is to be avoided.
I do not mean to imply that all of that $12,289 million of increase in our public holdings of liquid assets represents active purchasing power. It does not, all of it. But it is true to say that the full amount of that $12,289 million has been created in the form of active purchasing power at some time since 1939, with which the securities represented in the sum I have mentioned were purchased.
And so it is generally true to say that there has been no less than $12,289 million expansion of currency and credit through the banking system since 1939. As I have already pointed out, to anyone with a mentality of abundance, a mentality geared to believe that this country can produce and deliver goods and services as, when ana where they are required to the extent of $12,289 million, that is not ah astounding figure at all. But most certainly the minister of finance in 1939 did have his mentality geared to scarcity and not to abundance.
In concluding this part of my remarks I should like to ask what would be the difference between the method of expanding the money supplied through the selling of bonds to the chartered banks, as was done largely during world war II, and the so-called inflationary method, through the creation by the government of additional supplies of money and their use to purchase what the government needs.
That is a good question, and it requires to be answered. As I see it, the only real difference is that in the end the Canadian people find themselves paying large sums in interest in perpetuity to the chartered banks, when we use the bond and chartered bank method of adding to the money supply. A considerable saving in taxation-that is, interest first, and taxation-could be saved for the Canadian people if the government would use its own machinery for the creation of any additional money supply that is required. I think that the supply could be kept much more carefully under control, and could be handled by a government agency so that we would not be constantly in danger of serious inflation or deflation.
Concluding my remarks I should like to add just a word or two about the interesting statement made by the minister the other day in his budget speech about government policy. He referred to the policy that was to be following during this period of emergency-and perhaps properly so. We Social

The Budget-Mr. Low Crediters were very much interested in what the minister called the pay as you go policy, which he defined in these words:
A pay as you go policy means that we as a government must fully and amply cover the whole of our expenditure by taxation and other budgetary revenues. In the present circumstances of high employment and active business this is the only honest financial policy. To plan to do less than this would be both irresponsible and a fraud on the public.
Both the Minister of Finance and the hon. member for Greenwood quoted from that same speech in 1939 by the former minister of finance, Mr. Ilsley. Both appear to think that that speech stands as a classic, particularly in so far as it expresses the pay as you go policy. The hon. member for Greenwood had this to say in an earlier debate of this session as it is reported at page 184 of Hansard for September 2:
The speech-
He is referring to the speech of the former minister of finance.
-goes on to say that when an economy is below its maximum a certain amount of credit inflation could be justified, and in fact they did have some in the autumn of 1939; but that was because things needed stimulating; that was because industry was at a somewhat low level, the absolute antithesis of the situation which we have now. This is the final quotation that I wish to read:
Then he read this from Mr. Ilsley's speech:
With an economy at full production and employment the only result of expanding money and credit is to raise prices without increasing production. At such a point commences the cumulative spiral of inflation with all its deadly consequences to the economy.
Having completed that quotation, the hon. member concluded with these words:
I suggest that those who made this decision seem to have forgotten September 12, 1939. It seems that this logic is irresistible. It seems to me that what I have read applies in the most inescapable manner to the situation of today. It seems to me quite clear that what has been done is exactly the opposite of what was considered to be the wise thing as set out at that time.
I like the hon. member for Greenwood. I have the highest respect for him. I think he is a nice fellow and I enjoy his company. I hope we shall always have the advantage of associating with intelligent men of that kind. But from what I have heard him say quite often in the house about financial policy, I can only get down on my knees and thank heaven he is not minister of finance. If he were, I feel certain that his capability long before this would have been turned to measures to reduce the amount of purchasing power in circulation among the Canadian people. In other words, I am satisfied that long ago he would have introduced a policy of deflation. Under our present system there is only one way of doing that kind of job and that is by deliberately imposing upon

the Canadian people a policy of unemployment. There is no other way. I hope my hon. friend will never become minister of finance as long as he maintains his present attitude, or at least until he releases his mind from the creeping scarce money philosophy that makes him ever to think in terms of bringing down the volume of money rather than bringing up the volume of production of goods and services.
I am persuaded that the present high cost of living cannot be said to be, in any substantial degree, the result of the volume of effective purchasing power in Canada. I am afraid I have wandered a bit from what I started out to consider, namely the rather mysterious policy called by the Minister of Finance the pay as you go policy.
Just what is it? I have been trying to find out. Mr. Ilsley is given the credit for enunciating the policy and hon. members can read what he had to say. I do not intend to take the time to quote his remarks, but they can be found at page 156 of Hansard of September 12, 1939. There are two ways of looking at this pay as you go policy. The first is from the point of view of the nation in relation to other nations. If we do not borrow from other nations, if we live within ourselves as a nation, then I suppose we can be said to be on a pay as you go policy.
The second way of looking at it is from the point of view of the government keeping its expenditures wholly within its budgetary revenue. The latter one appears to be the type mentioned by Mr. Ilsley. He had reference to a policy of financing the war effort by a combination of taxation and borrowing from the Canadian people and the chartered banks. The figures I have given show how far we have gone in that borrowing policy. Certainly that policy cannot truly be called a pay as you go policy. If Mr. Ilsley had really introduced such a pay as you go policy, then I ask this question: How come the national debt has increased since 1939 by something like $12,000 million?
The fact is that there has been no pay as you go policy by this government or by any government in Canada except that of the province of Alberta. I say that seriously. The government of that province has really kept its expenditures within its budgetary income. It has not borrowed a single dollar from anybody in the thirteen years since 1937, and in that time it has paid off $50 million of its debt. That in reality is a pay as you go policy.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That was applied before we discovered oil.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is a policy to which I wholeheartedly subscribe. I should like to see the minister adopt such a policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They did not have to fight a war in Alberta.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But this government has the mechanism to handle it without borrowing a dollar, and the minister knows that. I had a hand in establishing the policy in Alberta, and we had a war on there too-a war against poverty. Moreover, I am convinced that this government should and could operate on a real pay as you go policy if it would make use of the sovereign powers that have been given to it under the constitution to create for itself the new money that may be required to keep the economy of Canada strong and healthy and our people happy and busy and secure.
I say in conclusion that if that kind of policy were to be applied and faithfully followed, taxation in Canada could become an instrument very largely to be used to prevent inflation by drawing off redundant or excess purchasing power.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as this parliamentary session is being pushed relentlessly forward to a speedy end the question arises in my mind, as it probably does in the minds of other hon. members, whether my duty is to be better accomplished by silently approving the decisions of the government in order to conclude our sittings expeditiously, or by expressing my views, for whatever they may be worth, on the momentous steps taken by the executive in the present crisis, steps which we have been asked to support and have already approved by our previous votes.
I for one would feel remiss in my duty to my constituents if I did not at a moment like this voice a few observations which come to my mind.
As for the executive, its duty was accomplished when after careful consideration, and evidently being in possession of more information than it cared or seemed able to give us at the outset, it introduced a series of measures to the house. We, the legislative body, have been asked to give the force of law to the implementation of such policies as the government has seen fit to adopt, and we are now being asked to approve the means of meeting the financial needs of the administration.
The desire of avoiding procrastination and of expediting the work of the house is commendable, and no one will find fault with it; but I am convinced that this desire had not as its object the curtailing in any way of the fullest expression of opinion on the part of
The Budget-Mr. Picard the elected representatives of the people at a time when such important measures are being submitted to them. Otherwise it would help to defeat the very aim we are professing to wish to achieve, that is, the protection of our democratic liberties.
It is therefore with a keen sense of carrying on the task which has been entrusted to me by my constituents that I shall make use of the time at my disposal with no remorse for contributing slightly to delaying perhaps the adoption of measures which will confirm the urgent steps already taken, and which will not be delayed or impaired even if the members of the executive are detained a little longer within the precincts of this assembly and not allowed to return immediately to the privacy of their departmental offices.
I shall not attempt to follow the previous speakers in their criticism of the resolutions introduced in the budget, nor shall I at this stage make extensive remarks as to what should be done next year to meet the expected vast expenditures we may be called upon to undertake. As it is, the budget has been well received in the country. It is a luxury tax budget. It is true, as some have said, that it is not enough to curb inflationary tendencies, but we should realize that it will take some time before the sums to be spent for rearmament reach the circulation stage. The effect on the national economy will not be felt before we have the opportunity to consider next year's budget.
My only suggestion for next year is that the income tax exemption levels be not lowered so that those who were not in a position to provide reserves for rainy days, or who experienced lower earning rates in the last two years, or even unemployment, may be given a chance in the years to come to recoup themselves and to average a reasonable income over a five-year period.
I intend today to consider the world situation that made this budget necessary and motivated in part our being summoned to Ottawa. I consider that I shall be following the tradition that in this debate a member may discuss any problem that influenced the introduction of the budget resolutions. Whether we like it or not, we cannot but face the fact that we in this House of Commons are taking positive steps today to embark Canada anew on military adventures. The dies are cast and we are preparing against the possibility of war. Of course we have done so, as always, with the loftiest ideal of maintaining peace, and simply applying the old principle, which we all learned at school, si vis pacem, para helium-if you want peace, prepare for war. It is, however, a well-known fact that preparedness has never prevented

The Budget-Mr. Picard war, but it may be noted that it has sometimes postponed it, and it surely has put nations who resorted to it in a better position when war came.
Nevertheless let us not delude ourselves. During the present session we are in the same position as the parliaments that sat in 1900, 1914 and 1939. The only difference is that at this time war is not to be declared, but our acts will have the same bearing upon the life of the country as those of the legislators who sat here on the eve of the South African and the two world wars. I think it would be rendering a bad service to the government and the country if we failed to realize the importance of our acts, and if our conduct could lead the government to believe that it is with enthusiasm and lightness of heart that we give our support to its decisions. It is with the greatest reluctance that I see Canada plunging ahead, abreast of the two great English-speaking empires and ahead of most of the other nations of the world, in the preliminary stages of a third world war.
I do not for one moment, however, support the views expressed by some members that we should not take the utmost precautions to ensure our safety, and that we should wait until our shores are threatened before we act. It is evident that it would then be too late. The lessons of the last war, as well as the march of events in Europe at the close of the war, should be enough to teach u* that our safety is tied to that of the other democratic nations. It is also evident that it is our duty to support all measures to strengthen our position and give evidence to possible aggressors that, in community with other free nations, we are determined to act jointly and with solidarity to resist any attempt from any source to gobble the world piece by piece, as was attempted by Hitler during the last war and as has been done in devious ways by the Soviet union since the close of the war.
With few exceptions-and fortunately they are remarkably few-we are all in agreement on that score. Where we differ is on the question how we should do it, by what methods we can better serve the common cause and ensure our own safety. How do we stand today? In a period of crisis when the world has nearly abandoned hope of ever seeing peace firmly established, when it is restless and worried as to what tomorrow may bring, Canada again must decide on the course it is to follow. This time the formal aims of the democratic nations are nearer their real aims than ever before. It is a well known fact that in any war, as well as in the acts of human beings generally, there are formal aims, those that you proclaim, and these are noble ones that may gain support. There are also the 
real aims that may not coincide with the others and may be less noble. In the South African war, for instance, the formal aims were very noble and the real ones less, as has been pointed out by many historians since the event; but in the present circumstances the formal aims, the defence of democracy and the defence of our liberties, are nearer the real aims, which are the defence of our own interests.
It is true that the survival of our own way of life is at stake, and that extends further than it may seem to. Our very standard of living, our economic welfare, is at stake because we are an exporting nation, and in a world dominated by Soviet Russia we may fare worse than in a world influenced by the United States. It is also true, and we must admit, that the struggle which threatens to engulf the whole world is one between two great imperialistic powers. While one aims at economic expansion and supremacy the other has a dual purpose, the spreading of communistic domination to help attain the soviet control of the world.
The dream that accompanied the birth of the United Nations five years ago soon vanished when Russia's lack of co-operation became apparent. But the weakness of the international organization goes back further to the concessions made at Yalta and Potsdam, and to the right of veto which was considered sacred not only by Russia but by each of the big five powers who enjoyed it. Let us be frank about it. The United States does not want to see its course charted by the small *nations any more than Russia does. If the United States felt that it would be systematically outvoted in the United Nations, it would not be any happier than Russia is, and might act differently.
In view of the fact that we cannot rely on the machinery of the United Nations to preserve the peace of the world, and in view of the evident resolution of the Soviets to extend their domination over the whole world, either directly, through the action of their satellites or through the action of the communist parties in other countries, subjected to the will of Moscow, more than ever we must realize that security can be assured only by collective action. To this end the government has committed Canada, and at the last election the people unequivocally approved of the actions of the government.
After a period of discussion in the United Nations we have come to the point where we must prepare to carry out our obligations. It has been said that there have never been any definite obligations on the part of Canada so far as the United Nations is concerned. It is quite true, as the Secretary of State for

External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) has admitted. Our more precise obligations are those we have assumed under the terms of the Atlantic pact; they also are not definite. Nevertheless moral obligations have been accepted in the name of our country. The fact that they are not definite gives even a greater responsibility to the government to decide on their scope. It is why the government should be all the more cautious in their approval of the proposals submitted to them, and in their approach to these problems as they come to the fore.
The discharge of their responsibility can be better effected by gearing the country for possible eventualities. This is why it would be folly to make too heavy commitments in this first flourish that has taken place in Korea. Canadians at large will all approve the extension of our armed services, and the sums of money intended for that purpose constitute the first premium on an insurance policy that may demand many more premiums in the years to come.
Acceptance of the principle of collective security involves the obligation to prepare for our own defence and for our share in the common task. That task may call for the presence of our troops in more than one spot if the whole pattern of Soviet expansion develops, as may be expected, at all points which we may forecast. Would it be wise, therefore, as has been suggested by some hon. members opposite, to commit too much of our strength at one point? It will be for those who have the responsibility to decide on our course of action. A word of caution therefore may not be out of order.
It is also within the realm of possibility that pressure has been exerted on our government by the government of the United States to obtain heavy definite commitments. The tone of many publications, both United States and Canadian, reflect this possibility. A few weeks ago Time magazine contained this statement:
The Canadian government yielded last week to a mounting clamour to send Canadian ground troops to fight alongside U.S. forces in Korea . . . Diplomatic pressure on Ottawa increased along with the public outcry. Requests for Canadian ground forces came so urgently from the U.S. embassy in Ottawa and the Canadian embassy in Washington that some touchy Ottawa officials got their backs up.
The Financial Times of Montreal on September 8 contained an article signed "V.A.B.", which contained the following statement:
The United States is not too pleased by the Canadian response to the Korean situation thus far. They are not saying too much about it. But the general feeling is that they are doing most of the ball carrying. And they don't like it, and who can blame them?
The Budget-Mr. Picard There will have to be a little something more than a token demonstration of assistance before this thing is done.

speechtext: Who said that?

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The article is signed "V.A.B." These, of course, are the assumptions and expressions of opinion of newspapermen; nevertheless they are logical assumptions and opinions which are entertained by many. Personally I can see no reason why this country should blindly follow the lead of the United States in all matters, any more than it should have previously followed the lead of Great Britain; and I do not for a moment believe this government would freely adopt that policy. Mind you, I do not say this because of any antagonism to the United States. On the contrary-and in this I may surprise some of my hon. friends-I would not have the objection that is entertained by many hon. members of this house to the Canadian provinces becoming states of the union. Economically I think we might fare better if all the people north of the Rio Grande were citizens of one great united nation. As things are at the present time we experience most of the difficulties that may befall the United States citizen, without enjoying all the same privileges. However, that is an altogether different subject; I came to it while considering the possibility that Canada might become a United States satellite.
If we are to keep our government institutions as they are now; if we are to remain a separate national entity, let us not do so only in words, but let us act accordingly. Or if we are to receive our directions from Washington, let us send our representatives there and become Americans.
Many citizens of that country, especially those opposed to the present administration, claim that Washington has had no precise foreign policy since the war; that at best theirs has been a policy of expediency. It is evident that the policy of the United States government has been vacillating, that its post-war policies in the Far East have been marked by many blunders.
Wherever the responsibility lies for the difficult position in which we find ourselves, it is clear that it springs from the expansionist manoeuvres of the Soviets and their satellites, which were not counterbalanced by proper precautions on the part of the United States. Be that as it may, today we are faced with a situation which leaves us no choice. We must embark upon a program of preparedness, and on this point we seem to be in accord, with few exceptions.
It is interesting, however, to note in Canada the same pattern of events that was followed
618

The Budget-Mr. Picard in the previous wars; first newspaper propaganda, then the Tory press urging that we should go in ahead of everyone else. The same pattern has been followed this time, in the face of this new crisis. From the moment the United States government decided to interfere in Korea, and even before the United Nations accepted the United States proposal for intervention, the English-Cana-dian press advocated that we enter the fight immediately. Similarly, at the very first opportunity we heard the Tory leaders reproach the government for what they called the insufficiency of the measures taken, and the failure of the government to commit all our forces to the fight in Korea. Also true to fashion, all their supporters from Quebec, with the exception of one, have proclaimed the theory of non-participation, and have blamed the government for doing too much in the way of preparedness.
The same dual tactics adopted in the past by that party are again to the fore. In 1939 the only Conservative member in this house from Quebec, then member for Gaspe, Mr. Roy, took issue with his party, and also took the Liberals to task for doing too much, while his leaders accused the government of laxity, and of not doing enough. The same thing was done this year by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Courtemanche). I may say, however, that the general tone of the speech by his leader on September 1, and of the speech on September 4 by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), will bring more credit to his party than his own. But it is clear that once again, true to their traditions, the Conservatives from Quebec have a different policy from that of the Conservatives from the other provinces. The general trend of the party, however, has been to advocate plunging ahead into the melee, to a greater extent than anyone else.
As for the government, its position has been clearly stated by the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The government leaders, true to the Liberal tradition, have remained level-headed. They have considered and studied the steps that were advisable in the interests of the country, having due regard to our obligations under the United Nations and the Atlantic pact. We have ratified the decisions they have taken up to the present in this regard, and we are now called upon to give them the means with which to implement those decisions. I believe the speeches in this house by the Prime Minister on September 1 and by the Secretary of State for External Affairs on August 31 and September 4 should be widely circulated,

since they give such a comprehensive and clear idea of Canada's position and of the decisions of the government.
We have approved the sending of three destroyers and an air transport squadron, and of the recruiting of a certain number of ground troops, which up to the moment constitutes our commitments to the United Nations forces. These have been criticized by some opposition members as not sufficient. I for one prefer to accept the view expressed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs on September 4, when he said, as reported at page 222 of Hansard:
Among the countries that have responded effectively to the United Nations appeal, Canada takes a proud place and does not need to apologize to anybody for her action.
If we look at the commitments made by the other members of the United Nations who have answered the call of the secretary general we see that Canada, as usual, has done more than most others, of course with the exception of the United States, whose forces engaged in Korea are not included in the list I am about to give. This information has been extracted from reports and memoranda submitted by the United Nations secretariat as at the last week of August. These commitments are as follows: United Kingdom, 4,000 ground troops, plus two battalions already stationed at Hong Kong; Australia, 4,000 troops; New Zealand, 4,000 troops; nationalist China has offered three divisions, which up to the present have not been accepted; The Netherlands, two battalions; the Philippines, 5,000 men; Canada, 5,000 or 6,000, which figure has now been raised to 15,000; Bolivia, thirty army officers; Thailand, 4,000 men; Belgium, infantry forces not specified; El Salvador, volunteers to be trained in the United States; Panama, volunteer troops unspecified; Turkey, 4,500 combat troops; France, 800 infantrymen.
So far as ships or air forces are concerned, the commitments are as follows: United Kingdom, undetermined naval forces, including carriers; Australia, three naval vessels and a fighter squadron; Canada, three destroyers and an air transport squadron; New Zealand, two frigates; The Netherlands, one destroyer; Norway, merchant shipping, not specified; France, one sloop; South Africa, one fighter squadron; Belgium, air transport, unspecified; nationalist China, naval escorts and air transport, not accepted as yet.
So far as economic and medical aid is concerned we have the following: Denmark, medical ambulance unit; Nicaragua, foodstuffs and raw materials; Philippines, medical supplies and foodstuffs; Sweden, field hospital; Liberia, natural rubber to the amount of

$10,000; Israel, medical aid; Lebanon, $50,000 for war relief; India, ambulance and surgical units; Panama, training grounds and air bases.
This should serve as an answer to those who think we have not done enough, and should demonstrate that Canada, following tradition, has again taken the lead. I cannot but note that the 6,000 men we first undertook to train have been increased to 15,000. I trust that our strategists will not overlook the possibility that other situations may demand our co-operation elsewhere, and that it might be wise policy to gear our action not in relation to the United States alone but also in relation to the other fifty-three members of the United Nations.
The first principle of collective security is to provide a measure of defence for one's own country, especially when, in our case, it might be that our own country will be one of the sore spots.
In the financial commitments that we approved last week there is an item that I am inclined to view with a certain amount of apprehension. It is the sum of $300 million for help to North Atlantic treaty nations. Is this a first step in a new so-called lend-lease program of the same nature as the one that was carried on during the last war? On September 5 the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) stated reservedly, as reported at page 299 of Hansard:
I have not mentioned here, though I have included it in that estimation, something out of another vote which is covered by this resolution, namely $300 million to be appropriated for assistance in the provision of equipment, facilities, services and the like to the North Atlantic treaty nations.
I wonder to which country this equipment will be given. Will it be the more needy, those whose standard of living is lower and who have more trouble, or to the more insistent, those who have better speakers near Ottawa to voice their demands. I wonder also how many countries outside the United States will thus act as Santa Claus to other North Atlantic treaty nations. I wonder also if we are thus establishing a precedent that will be renewed from time to time. I wonder if we can afford to start anew on the path of generosity, and how our budget will be influenced in years to come by handouts of $300 million. Mind you, I support the principle of collective security and our obligations to share the burden, but I am thinking also of the burden the taxpayer of Canada will have to shoulder if we go on playing millionaire because our neighbour happens to be a real millionaire.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer to an unsigned declaration distributed by
The Budget-Mr. Picard mail and by hand and purporting to represent the views of a delegation of the youth of the province of Quebec concerning the Korean expedition and the attitude of the government in the present crisis.
I think it is advisable to caution the youth and the whole people of my province against this literature. It is a fine specimen of Moscow-dominated communistic propaganda, subtly drafted in order to misrepresent facts. Some of the very arguments leading to the conclusion that Canada should sit complacently and do nothing are the very arguments that would prompt me to support a program of preparedness. I quote:
We love our country, our province.
So says the declaration, and it continues:
We know that we have responsibilities: to devote our energies to make our country prosperous, to make life better and happier through our work.
This is the aim of all Canadians, but in order that everyone may thus accomplish his task, we must ensure the security of the country, and the best way is through collective action. The declaration goes on to say:
We do not think the best way to make our lives useful is to offer them on foreign battlefields for foreign interests.
It is true that it is a pity that the young, the strong and the healthy should have to be called for the defence of the country; but it is the masters of those who drafted this declaration who make this compulsory by their agitation everywhere, by their keeping millions under arms in Russia, and by their arming and training hordes of fanatical supporters in other countries. When they mention foreign interests they try to assimilate the present emergency to the South African war or the first world war, in which in the minds of many in my province, Canadian soldiers fought for, let us call them, foreign interests more than for national safety. Yet I am convinced that people cannot be misled today; they understand that if Canada must carry its share of the burden on foreign battlefields, it is because it understands that collective defence is today the only safeguard of individual security.
The conclusion of that declaration is such that I can agree with it word for word, but because I put the right interpretation or meaning on the words. The declaration says:
We ask today: No Canadian lives for Korea, but an independent Canadian policy that will help to maintain peace in the world.
"No Canadian lives for Korea"; I agree, because I maintain that if any lives are lost in Korea it will not be for Korea but for
620

The Budget-Mr. Picard Canada, in order to make sure that what happened in Korea will not happen in Canada.
"An independent Canadian policy"; again I agree. It is in perfect independence that we must pursue our course of action, the same as all the North Atlantic treaty nations, the same as all the United Nations who up to now have answered the call, convinced as we all are that we shall be able to remain independent only if we are not subjected to the threats and the blackmail of the Soviets. "A policy that will help to maintain peace in the world"; again I agree, because I consider that the best chance the world has to avoid war is by showing to the Soviets that all the nations of the world still enjoying liberty will resist collectively.
A period of appeasement has brought no good results. Each new move to expand Soviet influence in Europe through their disguised intervention has been followed by more intrigue and the evidence of newer ambitions. Militarily, Russia is more powerful today than any other nation in the world, and their friends would of course like the other nations of the world not to be in a position to face and to repulse Soviet strength if it is ever used.
Mind you, this declaration has been circulated widely up to now, even though we received it in the mail only today. That same declaration has been distributed in our villages and elsewhere. My answer to these peace lovers is this. Let Russia admit within its borders United Nations commissions to check on her armaments. Let Russia give the world the assurance that it is disarming, and the evidence that it is, and the rest of the world will not talk about armaments; they will not talk about arming. Let Russia accept the principle of survey and inspection within her territory of her atomic research projects, and then the United States may accept the destruction of her bombs. Let us answer our apostles of peace that if Russia wants to remain just as disarmed proportionately as Canada is today, we will then believe in the good will of these Canadian apostles of peace.
I do not think it is advisable to justify our attitude in this present crisis solely on the question of ideology, although it may carry great weight in our minds. The maintenance of our security, and even of our standard of living and our ways of life, should appeal even more to every young man in this country. Also, to be quite frank, I do not think that the fight in Korea is waged mainly to ensure free democratic institutions for Koreans. As I said before, that may be one aim. If this is the sole aim of the destruction


carried on in South Korea now, it will fall short of its realization, because there will not remain much to be democratized once the fight is over.
The Russians could not choose a better spot in which to test the American reactions to their war by proxy. I am led to believe that barely a year ago the American authorities had never entertained the idea of defending South Korea. Were it otherwise, it would be hard to explain their lack of preparedness. That a change of mind came suddenly upon the Americans seems evident, and we are now all called upon to suffer for their earlier blunders; the sad thing is that we cannot avoid being brought into that mess.
American policy is all the more surprising with regard to Formosa. We all must admit that, although we are all sympathetic to them. While Chiang still controlled considerable proportions of the mainland of China, it became the right thing in Washington to discredit Chiang's government for its inefficiency, for the graft of some of its officials, for its lack of democratic practices and tendencies; and no help, or nearly none, was given to him when there was still hope that he could hold firm. Now that he controls only Formosa; now that the whole of the mainland is reorganized or in process of reorganization under Mao, the United States want to defend Formosa, and refuse to accept as a reality the changes that have occurred on the mainland.
On this score also let us not delude ourselves. What has happened in the Far East is more than a Russian-abetted manoeuvre. Little of what happened in the Far East since the end of the war could have been realized if the people had not been co-operating with it.
One should not be accused of accepting Soviet propaganda because he recognizes these facts. Walter Lippmann and many other unbiased students of international affairs have long entertained these thoughts and they cannot be accused of communistic tendencies.
If Canada's decision in this crisis had been motivated only by a single cause, the invasion of southern Korea, I would be far less inclined to approve of these measures. But no one can ignore the fact that the Korean incident is but a test case and may be the first of many such expansionist moves by Soviet Russia. What induces me more to approve of the measures submitted to us is that they are part of a program of preparedness that is unavoidable in the present world circumstances, and everybody will understand that.

I quite realize that some people might be tepid in their feelings about the Korean adventure if considered strictly in itself, but nobody can blind himself to the reality of the situation at large. All nations of the world who like and care for their present ways of life must take the necessary steps to try and defend them. That they should not be led blindfolded by befuddled United States officials is another thing, as I mentioned a moment ago; that all nations should have as their first object their own interests goes without saying, but it remains for those who have been entrusted with the conduct of the nation to consider, weigh and decide, as Laurier said in 1900; and I for one have more confidence in the Prime Minister and his principal colleagues than in the leaders of the Tory party not to lose sight of the true perspectives and not to embark Canada on perilous unjustified adventures. I have more confidence in the Prime Minister's decision as to what should be done to ensure the safety and the prosperity of Canada.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to follow the hon. gentleman's arguments about Korea, and Canada's participation in that action. I have spoken before on this subject in this session, and what I said then stands. There are certain things nevertheless that he said that I should like to comment on. We must realize, and realize very clearly at the present moment, that the war in Korea is not something we have any choice about. If our signature as a free nation, and a member of the United Nations, means anything it means that our responsibilities demanded that we should play our part in putting down aggression in Korea.
There cannot be any escape from that responsibility for any Canadian, no matter where he comes from. It is a matter not only of our national honour but our very survival. The sad fact is that if we win in Korea we still may have a general war; but if we lose in Korea it is very certain we shall have a general war; and for that reason, if for no other, I feel the action taken by the government, while belated, and while in my opinion not resolute enough, was unavoidable. I cannot see any freely elected government in Canada reneging on its solemn obligations, or being foolish enough to believe that we had no responsibilities to preserve our very existence in putting down or helping to put down aggression in Korea. Korea is the erupting boil on the skin of the iron curtain, but there are approximately twenty thousand miles of frontier of the iron curtain countries, expanding from Korea right
The Budget-Mr. Adamson down through Asia and ending in Finland, which may erupt at any time. Large portions of this dangerous perimeter are the responsibility of the other free nations. Canada has undertaken nothing elsewhere in that large perimeter. We have no forces assisting our allies in the occupation of Germany, which is now not an occupation force, but a defence of Europe force. We have not assisted in any of the operations in southeast Asia and all along that frontier between the free and the slave world.
Unless we are prepared to play our part as an adult nation, not just by talk, but by action, our right to exist as a free nation will be taken from us, and I regret to say by force. There is no alternative. There is a saying which I think is a biblical one, and which I shall slightly paraphrase, namely, that when I was a boy I spoke as a boy, but now I am a man I put away childish things.

speechtext:
Well, the childish belief apparently held by the minister that we can live isolated to ourselves, without taking responsibility for preserving the collective peace of the world, is one of the beliefs which we must put away.
Less than a month ago a famous gentleman, the prime minister of Australia, made a speech in Ottawa. He spoke of the democracies,-or, preferably the free nations, because the word democracy has now been so prostituted, owing to the way it is bandied about by the communist party, that I prefer the expression "free nations", where the individual is assured of his freedom.
Menzies said there were three jobs to do. One was to prepare to resist aggression, the second was to expand our economy, and the third was to prevent inflation from destroying us. It is with this third problem I wish to deal today. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has admitted the problem in what I shall call the carbonated beverage budget. He has imposed luxury taxes, taxes on soft drinks, and taxes on other certainly nonessential goods.
I thought he perhaps was reminded-if he was not I will remind him now-of a poem by the late G. K. Chesterton, two stanzas of which might aptly be quoted with reference to this problem. The first of these is:
Feast on wine or fast on water And your honour shall stand sure,
God Almighty's son and daughter,
He the valiant, she the pure;	[DOT]
If an angel out of heaven Brings you other things to drink,
Thank him for his kind attentions,
Go and pour them down the sink.

The Budget-Mr. Adamson
The last verse, which I shall slightly paraphrase, is this:
As for all the windy waters,
They were rained like tempests down When good drink had been dishonoured By the tipplers of the town;
When red wine had brought red ruin And the death-dance of our times,
Heaven sent us Coca Cola As a torment for our crimes.
I think we can regard these minor tax changes as temporary palliatives and view them in the rather light-hearted way indicated by G. K. Chesterton in his poem. But as a stop for inflation and as a measure really to meet the problems we are facing today, with all due respect to the minister, they are practically without effect.
Inflation is simply the relationship between the supply of goods and the supply of money. There can be no other way in which inflation takes place, except by the dislocation of this relationship. Despite what the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) has said, if you increase your money supply and do not increase your supply of goods, you are always going to have inflation, anywhere in the world. If you have $10 and one hundred potatoes the relation between the $10 and the potatoes is so much. If you have $100 and a thousand potatoes, the relationship is the same. But if you have $20 and one hundred potatoes, then the relationship between the money and the potatoes changes radically. That, more or less, is what has happened to our economy since the war. The supply of money to the supply of goods has altered by about two to one so, instead of having $10 and one hundred potatoes we now have $40 and two hundred potatoes, with the hypothetical relationship betwen the dollar and the potato being now about five to one instead of the ten to one it was in 1939. Therefore, theoretically at least, the dollar buys less, by about one-half of what it did pre-war.
There are, however, slightly modifying factors. But if one will look at the supply of goods and the increase in the money supply and the increase in the cost of living he will find they bear the same close relationship as the theoretical case I have indicated in connection with potatoes. This simple example shows clearly exactly what has actually happened in Canada.
War always causes inflation because the goods produced are for destruction and not for use. That is the very essential feature of war: the goods are destroyed, but the money which went to produce them remains. Therefore money increases but the supply of goods does not.


The Keynesian theory of government spending to keep full employment going is progressive continuous inflation. The pursuit of that theory in the era of greater government spending for national defence has set up the impetus which will bring the whirlwind of inflation.
I shall make a suggestion to the minister in a moment. At the present time, however, we see our cost of living approaching 170, our money supply approaching four and a half billions and our production approximately twice what it was, giving a relationship of money supply to production of about two to one. We see the wages in industry approaching $1.50 per hour, and in skilled trades very much higher than that. We see meat at $1 a pound, and other goods increasing in price in about the same ratio.
This means that if we are not going to see the sort of thing of which I am most fearful, some drastic action will have to be taken. That will have to be done if we are not going to see wages approaching $5 an hour-and that figure is not out of the question because I saw where at one point in the United States skilled tradesmen were getting $4.50 an hour for their work.
As these prices increase there is a large segment of the population of the country that faces absolute ruin, and unless we can in some measure put a stop to inflation at the present time we are not going to be able to preserve the economic system which we call free. Unless the whole economy is controlled, controls do not give the answer. If the whole economy, which would include prices, wages and everything else we buy, sell or do, is controlled, then we are not living in a free world. That is one of the things we are fighting against. As I said, unless we can prevent inflation going to the utmost limit our free society is destroyed. Hon. members must know that the communist primer, Lenin's writings, states that one sure way of destroying the capitalist free world is through the use of inflation. Therefore, it is of the utmost importance that steps be taken now to combat this great danger and evil.
It is a two-pronged problem that we face. One prong is the necessity to reduce the supply of money. To impose taxation by forced savings and to raise the bank rate is certainly one method. But if you shrink the supply of money by such arbitrary methods you are going to cause great damage to the population, in fact no freely elected government in Canada could do it, and survive. By deflation you will bring about a dislocation of the economy, with devastating results,

particularly to the hourly wage earner. Therefore, the methods used in the dictator countries cannot be considered in Canada.
The second prong of the battle against inflation is to increase the production of the country. While we have increased our production the fact is that our productivity has not increased as fast as the money supply. The disparity between these two things is the measure of the inflation we are suffering today. These things must be understood. Increased productivity can be brought about only by greater efficiency, and harder work.
The reduction in the money supply can be achieved however in several ways. The international monetary fund has decided to keep the statutory gold price at $35 in terms of United States dollars. In my opinion that is a misguided attempt on the part of the international monetary fund to combat inflation. Nevertheless they have taken that step and in consequence the flight from the United States dollar during the last few months has been considerable. The flow of gold from Fort Knox may force the United States to abandon any pretence that they are related to gold and stop even the foreign holders of U.S. currency, either governments or individuals, from converting it into gold. In recent weeks American purchases on the Canadian stock markets, have amounted to very substantial sums. Tremendous buying of Canadian equities by United States nationals has been going on and there is evidence that this is another symptom of the problem facing that country.
We have relaxed our controls and curbs on the purchase of American goods. Owing to the present war, and for other reasons, our trade with the United States is becoming more and more in balance. We are having, and will have, progressively more of the raw materials and metals and other things that the United States must have for its economy. Therefore, I envisage the time when the balance of trade may run the other way and in our favour. The continued buying of materiel necessary for the preservation of peace will I suggest go a long way toward solving the problem of any dollar shortage we might have. Incidentally I was glad to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) state the other day that the exchange rate as between Canada and the United States is not going to be altered by government action.
Coming now to my suggestion to decrease the money supply. I suggest to the minister that there be established a futures market in gold so that Canadian nationals could buy gold now which would be earmarked for
The Budget-Mr. Adamson delivery in 1952, on or after the statutory expiry date of the emergency legislation we have enacted this session, delivery of the gold to be taken in two years' time in the form of minted bullion with no restrictions upon what the owner did with it. The government would have the use of the money for two years without interest. The result would toe that those people who wanted security later on would pay money to the government in order to have the security that goes with the holding of gold. The government would merely issue a promise to pay so many ounces of gold on a given date.
The surplus money that is causing so much trouble at the present time would be used up in the purchase of futures certificates for gold. It would drain off painlessly the present surplus purchasing power which is exerting such a pressure on scarce consumer and capital goods. The receipts would be non-negotiable, and could not be borrowed on at the bank, as in the case of our present bank stock scrip. The effect would be to create a stabilizing force so far as our currency is concerned. The production of gold for the first six months of the year is 2,200,000 ounces. Therefore production is at the rate of about four and a half million ounces a year. If two million ounces of gold were earmarked for purchase at the statutory price of $38.50 per ounce it would mean that an immediate reduction of the money supply by voluntary means of between $75 million and $80 million would take place. In view of the consumer credit bill passed by the house last night, I suggest that would materially help to relieve the pressure.
If our trade with the United States is in balance the government could not put the gold to better use than to provide this safety valve against inflation. It would mean that in a two-year period, or within the period of emergency, the sum of over $150 million would be removed painlessly from our money supply if we used half of our annual production of gold. It would be done voluntarily and the government would have the use of the money interest free for the period of two years. The holders of the scrip would toe unable to borrow against it and by so doing increase inflationary pressure.
I submit that such a plan would be of tremendous assistance in relieving the pressure on consumer goods. The advantages to the individual are of course a hedge against inflation. It has been and is the present policy of Canada, and all other signatories to the international monetary fund agreement, to maintain the present price of gold.
624	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Sinclair Therefore let us not go into the question of whether gold would rise or decrease in value, because it is the joint policy of this monetary body to keep gold at the present statutory price.
Another group of people who would benefit would be the holders of insurance policies. If the holders of such policies maturing two years or more from now could take advantage of machinery whereby when the policies were paid off they would be paid in gold, it would be of great assistance to them. Insurance company representatives came before a committee of the house during the last session and said that they had an obligation in dollars to their policy holders, and that obligation was in dollars irrespective of what the purchasing power of the dollar might be when the policies were paid off. Here again would be a safeguard against a decreased value of insurance policies at the time of maturity. I submit that the assistance to trade by freeing gold to Canadian individuals and corporations would be a very great advantage.
The suggestion I have made would only help to solve one part of the great problem. Productivity must be increased. The money supply must be restricted. If these things are not done there is no other answer than the destruction of our whole economic system through inflation. That is the communist goal. We can put ourselves into a complete strait-jacket by controlling wages, restricting purchases, controlling prices, and instituting control of our economy so rigid that we would destroy our freedom. We can risk the destruction of our economy by inflation or we can take voluntary steps now to avoid both the terrible courses facing us in the future.
