maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it would be expected that I should speak briefly in this budget debate. The present session has been quite an unusual one in one way, the great number of opposition speakers and the comparative fewness of the government speakers. As the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. Carroll) said this morning, that is not an indication of lack of interest but an indication that the Liberal party is solidly behind the government in their program at this time. Therefore there is no need for us to do other than support their policies by vote. However admirable that policy of restraint may be for most government members, I find that I chafe at the bit somewhat when I sit here and listen to some of the arguments which have been made because of this open season for opposition speakers. Today I am going to spend a 

little time on the speeches that have been made by the official financial Critic of the Conservative party and by the new financial critic of the C.C.F. party. I found, of course, as I am sure most hon. members found who heard the financial critic of the Conservative party, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), speak after the budget was delivered on Thursday night and again this morning, that we had heard the speech before, because underlying it was his usual understandable sense of frustration. Here he was, having to put up a show of criticizing a budget which once again, in the interval between its presentation and his speech, had been clearly shown to be highly acceptable to the Canadian people. With that as a background one can understand that sense of frustration.
The hon. member in his speech used a baseball analogy as far as the minister is concerned. This is a great football town, I think the most enthusiastic in Canada, and perhaps I may be excused if I use an analogy taken from football. The hon. member is a great Monday morning quarterback. After the game is over, on Monday morning the experts from the offices sit around their cups of coffee, and they can always play the game over much better than did the quarterback of the home team out on the field on Saturday afternoon, especially if his team lost. We had that kind of Monday morning quarterbacking this morning from the hon. member for Greenwood, in his speech on the budget.
There is one note that has always interested me in his speeches. I listened to his speech this morning, and also refreshed my memory as to speeches he made in previous years. Hansard is a great thing in that way. I find that he always uses a very nice approach, an approach which I am sure is used by many of us at political meetings. He starts off by telling some little anecdote, and thus breaking the ice. In the case of the hon. member, just before making his budget speech he always meets some man who, in some simple way, with an innocent remark completely devastates the government. I often wish these men he meets would be elected as Conservative members, because if they were here and spoke as effectively as they do in his anecdotes I am sure we would have a much better opposition. However I am going to take a leaf out of his book and tell the house about a man I met not long ago who had a little anecdote to tell. He was a Conservative, and he was anxious about the future of the Conservative party. He met a Conservative member and asked, "What is the policy of the Conservative party today?" Like little Audrey, the answer of the Conservative member was to just laugh and laugh and laugh.

If hon. gentlemen opposite want examples of that sort of thing I can give them very quickly. They came in here with no policy for dealing with the rail strike and so struck out in all directions. Hon. members on this side of the house could watch the face of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) as, during the debate and the votes in connection with the rail strike legislation, Tory after Tory announced that he had his own policy and that he would vote accordingly with the government. We felt it was worth while coming here if only to watch the expression on the face of the hon. gentleman as he heard these desertions but dared not turn around to see who else was leaving him. Then we had a Conservative, the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Courtemanche), declare himself absolutely isolationist against aiding the United Nations in Korea. The two independent Conservatives from Quebec, the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon) and the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Poulin), have also proclaimed themselves isolationists. They may not call themselves Conservatives, but certainly they ran against Liberal candidates and they vote and act like Conservatives. Then we have a new isolationist in this house, the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), who publicly urged no veterans to enlist for service in Korea. A moment ago I heard some comment by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), who is one of the great constitutional lawyers in the house, or so he says. I have a little legal problem I would be glad to have him solve. What is the difference between another Conservative, the mayor of a city, who urges people not to register during a time of war, and who goes to internment camp as a result, and a member of parliament who urges veterans not to enlist to fight a war that is our common war?
To get back to finance, I said that the task of the hon. member for Greenwood was difficult. It was especially difficult because that morning the newspaper generally regarded across Canada as the official voice of the Conservative party, the Globe and Mail, carried an editorial in which it called upon Mr. Abbott to make no changes in the existing tax structure; to do no tinkering with the budget; to just carry on, even if it meant a small deficit. The evening the budget was delivered and again this morning the official financial critic of the opposition, giving the other Conservative viewpoint, gave the impression that what he wanted was to create a sense of urgency by having much bigger taxes at this time.
Here again I realize the advantage of having a good memory, as far as previous speeches by the hon. member are concerned.
The Budget-Mr. Sinclair I remember that two years ago, when the minister was continuing the wise policy of fairly heavy taxation following the war, when times were good, in order to siphon off excess purchasing power when goods were in short supply and in order to pay the debts we incurred during the war, the hon. member used very different words. Did he ask then for more and heavier taxation? No; he said the minister was mulcting the public out of money which was theirs. At that time the Tory press called this wise policy barefaced thievery. Today it is different, of course; the hon. member has changed his mind, just as the Conservative party changes its policy so often it is hard for us to keep track of the official line of the moment.
Then there is the economy cry; that was the next thing in his speech. I sat on the public accounts committee last session with the hon. member, the leader of the opposition and quite a number of other opposition members. A very careful scrutiny of the public accounts was carried on with all the ability and all the advice they could get; and the only practical economy move I heard suggested came from the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher), who said we could save $2 million every ten years by doing away with the prairie census, which is taken between the regular censuses. I must admit, though, that this morning the hon. member for Greenwood came up with a new economy measure. He would do away with the publicity branch of the Post Office Department. Well, I took time to find' out what is done by this publicity branch. It is a very small department, which gives the people of Canada information about postal rates, as to when they should mail Christmas parcels, as to what sort of mail can be sent airmail, as to what requires airmail stamps and what is carried by airmail at normal rates. Abolition of that sort of useful information service was the kind of economy measure which in his speech this morning the hon. member for Greenwood thought would solve many of our fiscal problems.
Of course the reason it is so difficult for him to find economies is the very tough job that has already been done by treasury board. I think all hon. members of this house at one time or another have run up against treasury board. Each of us at some time or other has had a desirable project in hand which would have meant so much to the people of our riding, but which we could not have carried out because treasury board put down its foot and refused to approve the expenditure. And despite this desire for economy I noticed that even after the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) had announced
626	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Sinclair that as an added measure we were going to have to do without quite a few capital expenditures that had ibeen planned, the junior member for Queens (Mr. McLure) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) rose to say, "Yes, but I hope that will not affect the post office in my town." Economy always starts in somebody else's riding.
Then the hon. member went on to deal with the estimates in the budget presented by the minister last spring, in which he estimated that there would be a surplus of $20 million. The surplus at the moment is very much higher than that, of course. It will drop by the end of the fiscal year, because our taxation collections are early and all our large expenditures are late; but even at that it is estimated that we will finish with a surplus of something like $180 million. Estimates are always difficult. It is fairly easy to estimate our expenditures pretty accurately, as we have done, because they are matters within our own control. It is very difficult, however, to estimate revenues when the actual sources of those revenues are subject to forces beyond the control of this or any other government. Therefore the Minister of Finance did what any good businessman would do and does every year; he overestimated his expenditures and underestimated his receipts, to be on the safe side-a very prudent course.
Once again in this connection I went back in my memory and thought we surely had some forecasts by the hon. member himself, so I read back in Hansard. Sure enough, back in the spring when the minister announced his budget forecast of $20 million, the hon. member had something to say himself on that subject. Today he is accusing the minister of having been too cautious and as a result having a much larger surplus than he estimated in the spring. At that time, however, deriding the estimated $20 million surplus which was forecast, at page 1519 of Hansard the financial critic said:
... if unemployment does not rise too much and trade does not go down too much we may break even.
That was his forecast last spring; he didn't think we would even break even. Now one other thing before I leave the hon. member. He said that here in this country today we had not a sense of urgency, that we were too complacent, that things were so different in Washington. Again one of these men he meets had told him that a man from Washington was appalled by the difference in outlook between Washington and Ottawa today. Well, I am a Canadian, and I was educated in the United States. I like the


Americans very much, but I want to say quite frankly that if this same man had gone from Ottawa to Washington in 1914 or 1915 or 1916 or in the spring of 1917, or in 1939 or 1940 or 1941, he would have been amazed and appalled at the very great difference in attitude between the capital at Ottawa and the capital at Washington. The Americans in their good time, in their way, did their part in those wars. We in our way with our own judgment shall do our part, because we have never failed in any war.
I now turn to the comments of the new financial critic of the C.C.F. party. This time I am going to use a baseball analogy like my friend the hon. member for Greenwood. He said about the minister that when he came to bat 'he had two strikes on him so far as the Conservative party was concerned. That was quite true. But fortunately the Conservative party in this country is not yet the government. However, the last financial critic of the C.C.F. party, their pitcher, has apparently been pulled out because he had taken too big a shellacking from the government side in previous years; and after the poor efforts of their new relief pitcher this morning, I think we will all agree that he spent too much time warming up in the bullpen. He had only three subjects, of which the first two had been mentioned endlessly on the hustings by the C.C.F. party: price control, excess profits tax, and a new one. He said personal income tax was too low. I am going to speak on that subject especially because that is a new official C.C.F. line.
I want to discuss these things, and I do not want to discuss them in the language of an economist because I am not one. I should like to look at them in the language of two members of the opposition who seem to convey more to their people about what goes on in parliament than any others: I refer to the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) and the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) who have this great gift of talking in terms that ordinary people understand. Today therefore, if I can, I should like to imitate them by talking about price control and about excess profits taxes in a way that the people of my riding will understand; and my riding is principally an industrial riding.
First of all, let us look at prices. What makes prices go up? The C.C.F. always has the easy answer: profiteering. That is, when it is companies who are concerned. But of course when farmers get higher prices and sell their beef at 28 J cents a pound on the hoof, which' the hon. member for Calgary West last night translated into a dollar a

pound to the housewife, that of course is not profiteering, because the C.C.F. remember that these people are farmers. They therefore describe it either as taking advantage of the market or as making up for the money they lost in the thirties. There is, I think, a little better formed answer to the question, namely the economists' answer: prices go up because too much money is chasing too few goods. That may be true academically but it does not make much sense to the housewife in my riding who knows that she has not too much money and who sees on the shelves of the stores plenty of goods which she would like to buy.
Let us turn now to the reason that I at least see for the rise in prices in this last period. In the old days of course, under a free economy, it was quite different. If prices went up, consumer resistance began and unsold goods began to gather. Other manufacturers saw an opportunity to get into a profitable field and started extra production. The law of supply and demand worked and down came prices. But this is no longer a free economy, because of the economic strains of the last war; and our expected expenditures on war industry and war equipment in the next year or two are going to accentuate the fact that this is no longer a free economy.
When we are siphoning off so much labour and so much material in war effort that is unproductive in the ordinary sense of the word, with goods in short supply today, there are two forces at work. One is demand for goods in short supply, drawing up prices; and there is a second force pushing them up, and that is the force of labour, because of the reaction of high prices on labour. Naturally high prices make the worker and his wife seek more money to meet those high prices, and so you have this double-edged effect today forcing up the prices of those goods which are in short supply.
Let us now have a look at what makes commodity prices in Canada. First and most obvious is the cost of the raw material in the product; second, there is the cost of labour; and third, there is the cost of plant and equipment which bring that raw material and labour together to create the manufactured product. Then there is a fourth item. Sometimes it is a profit if the demand for the product is good; sometimes it is a loss. But these are the four items that make up the cost of our normal consumer commodities today.
I am going to speak principally about consumer commodities because they have a slightly closer connection with the Department of Finance, and the capital goods have been dealt with by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). Let us look at the
The Budget-Mr. Sinclair above items in turn. If any one of these goes up, naturally the price of the finished commodity is going to be shoved up.
Let us take material costs first. The Curtis report on prices had an interesting analysis of the materials that went into what we ordinarily call consumer goods in Canada. Thirty per cent of the material in the ordinary consumer goods in Canada are of foreign origin. The cost of those goods is something over which this government has absolutely no control. If they come from countries in which there is no price control, then of course those prices will be high. If inflation is apparent in those countries the prices of that thirty per cent portion will go higher and higher and higher. We have not much hope of controlling the cost of that thirty per cent of material cost unless those countries adopt price control too. That is why the remarks made earlier in this debate have so much point today. We in this country cannot hope to have an effective system of price control unless our great neighbour to the south also has it. That was the secret of our price control in the last war; and even more so today. The American economy, through their vast productivity and through the Marshall plan, has a dominant effect on world prices. And there today-because of that thirty per cent factor of materials mostly from the United States, partly from Britain, other parts from other countries, and those countries of course have still higher costs- we encounter our first difficulty.
Our next trouble is this. It is not only the price of foreign imports which hoists up our material costs. It is our own exports to those foreign countries. I can give you one good example, namely lumber in my own province. There is a tremendous demand for British Columbia lumber in the United States today at a high price; and it is natural that if we are going to have free trade between our countries, then the domestic price is going to follow the high export price. To go into the next province, namely Alberta, exactly the same story is told about beef. One thing that amuses me is this. Some of the very members who today are complaining about the cost of beef are the very same members who a year or two ago were thundering away to have the embargo lifted on beef shipments to the United States.
Then there is a third effect of our material costs, the first cost in commodity prices, and that is undoubtedly the effect of our tremendous capital investment program. Since the end of the war we have had in this country tremendous investment in new factories, new mines, new oil wells, new public buildings, new private buildings, all these things in our expanding economy which are so necessary to
628	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Sinclair provide the added employment this country needs and wants in order fully to develop our resources. But these projects are competing not so much for the consumer goods but for the labour which would otherwise be used in producing consumer goods. I do not think there is a Canadian in Canada today who will say that where the rise in our prices is due to this great capital investment program it has not been worth while; because it has created great employment and as never before we are prepared on the industrial front.
The second principal cost in production I mentioned was this matter of labour cost. The first and most obvious cost is the direct labour cost. It varies. If I may use one of the principal industries in my own riding as an example, I will mention saw mills. After all, lumber is an important thing in Canada. The operators in my riding figure that about forty per cent of the cost of producing lumber in a saw mill is direct labour cost, but that is not the entire story. Other costs are the cost of materials and the cost of equipment. The material is logs. The cost of logs from logging camps amounts to a material cost to the saw mill man, but back in the logging camp the cost is broken down again into the costs of acquiring stumpage, and labour cost. My friend the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson), who should know, tells me that today in an up-to-date logging camp labour costs run fairly close to fifty per cent. There is also the labour involved in making the equipment used in the saw mills. I would say that if you added the direct labour costs in the factories, and the labour costs which are embedded in the material used and the plant and equipment necessary to produce, you will find that labour is generally at least half of the final cost of a product that is sold on the consumer market.
There are some, of course, who say that you can control prices without controlling labour costs. It is extremely difficult to prove to any thinking person, when labour costs are such an important part of the final commodity price, how that can be done. There are today two factors which increase labour costs. We have of course the spiral: higher prices make labour ask for more wages to meet those prices, which put prices up, and around it goes. It is like the chicken and the egg. It all depends on where you sit as to which came first. We know that, and the workingmen's families in this country know it especially well. Those in organized labour have been fortunate. They have shown their good sense in belonging to organized labour, because they have been able to bargain for


those necessary increases. But the more difficult classes of course are the white-collar workers and those on fixed incomes; they have not the same bargaining power and so they are alone on the end of the spiral.
But this is only one of the reasons why labour costs are being forced up. Internal and external demand for some goods also force up labour costs. Today in British Columbia, for example, because of the tremendous export market, our lumber mills, the logging mills and paper mills are doing very well, and the men who work for them know they are doing very well. If you believe in democracy at all, then you believe that capital and labour should both enjoy the fruits of that extra production. Labour therefore says to management, "All right, you are doing well; we want an increase in wages," something quite removed from their actual needs as compared, for example, with a person on superannuation. Because these companies are doing well and do not want strikes but want to keep in production, they do not put up the same resistance to wage increases as perhaps an employer would who was not making a profit. Therefore because of that export demand for B.C. lumber higher wages in this industry are obtained, and then in other industries the wage scale is pretty well set by the wage scale which the loggers, the sawmill workers, the pulp and paper mill workers have obtained. Other labour groups and other white-collar groups ask for the increases the loggers have received, and take it as their pattern, whether the company they work for is making money or not. So there again is another pressure shoving up labour costs and therefore commodity prices.
We find a similar pressure created because of internal demand here in the east. There is the demand for automobiles. The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) said this morning that there is still a great demand in this country for new automobiles. Because of that, the companies -are doing well and are anxious to stay in production. Then, for the same reason the employees of these companies say, "We should share in this extra money you are making"-as they should. Once again the pattern certainly for industrial labour here in eastern Canada is pretty well set by the increases won by the automobile workers because of the good profits made in that industry. These then are the two pressures forcing labour costs up: the natural desire to get more wages to meet higher prices, and the natural desire to share in good profits.
I know there -are people in this country who take all opportunities to advocate price

The Budget-Mr. Sinclair
control but make no mention of wage controls. An example of that was given in this House of Commons' not so very long ago and may be found at page 452 of Hansard. Hon. members would do well to look at this. The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Sinnott), who is a farmer representing farmers, asked the leader of the C.C.F. party a very simple question. He asked whether it was the policy of his party to believe in at this time over-all price and wage control. Instead of a short yes or no there are two paragraphs of the finest pussyfooting and evasion that have ever adorned the pages of Hansard. And when it was all done our farmer from Springfield said, "you still have not given a yes or no", and the leader of the C.C.F. party said:
I am afraid I cannot help it if the hon. member does not understand me; it is not my fault.
It certainly is not his fault that he does 'not understand. The leader of the C.C.F. party took great care in this statement to see that he did not understand. He skirted around wage control by saying that during the war wage control was enforced by labour itself on a voluntary basis. You remember at the beginning of the war we had that fine no-strike pledge voluntarily offered by labour, but once it became necessary to impose price controls, wage controls had to follow. Labour did co-operate, but it was not voluntary, and the wage scales were administered by the national war labour board, on which labour and management and the people of Canada, through the government, had representation. Therefore when he speaks of price control and makes no mention of wage control, then I say he is kidding the Canadian people.
I say at the moment that it is extraordinarily difficult to have a practical workable price control, as we had during the last war, first of all because of the fact that we have no control over thirty per cent of the basic materials which we use in consumer goods, and secondly because the Canadian people apparently are not ready for wage and salary controls which must inevitably follow. We need more than this, however, to have effective price control. You may have good regulations, but you must have skilled people administering them, and we certainly had that during the last year. It cannot be done by our civil servants, no matter how able they are, because they have been too remote from the very technical problems of production and marketing.
When you enforce an arbitrary price control across the country you are trying to dam tremendous economic forces which until then have flowed freely and adjusted themselves in countless ways every day in every business
deal across the country. If you are to have an effective dam, you must have the machinery, you must have the people who are intimately aware of the problems of industry and the forces to be controlled. In wartime they came down here, some dollar-a-year men, and some served on government salaries. They did a splendid job on the wartime prices and trade board. But despite their knowledge and all that, there was continuous trouble. One that I remember is that of baby clothes. There was no baby clothing in Canada because the price set on baby clothes was out of relation to the price set on children's wear and adults' wear. And the manufacturer, with only so much cloth and so much labour at his command, found he could do better with what he had by making children's clothes and adults' clothes.
The second step for effective price control is to recruit a corps of these extremely trained and able men, who today are in industry across the country. They came here in wartime. I do not know that they would be so willing and anxious to come now in peacetime when every business across the country is faced with great problems with which it has to grapple as we approach a showdown with Russia. There is another reason why I think that some of them will be a little reluctant to come down here.
During the war we had Donald Gordon from the Bank of Canada doing a magnificent job because he had the guts to stand up against the manufacturers and say, "This is the price; this is what it is going to be, and that is it", and also because he had the confidence and respect of those businessmen who came in contact with him and who knew he would give able and fair decisions. Donald Gordon took another job, a job in which he was again going to try to represent the people of Canada, to try to make their Canadian National Railways a success, to try to hold freight rates so the consumers of this country and the farmers of this country would get a better break. When it came to the time of labour negotiations, the union leaders did the job they were picked for and spoke for the men, and Donald Gordon spoke for the job he was picked for, namely, to try to hold costs and so rates on the Canadian National Railways, which incidentally runs at a loss, the same job any other manager negotiating for his company would try to do. But what happened? He is abused and he is blackguarded in this house by members of the opposition, including the leader of the C.C.F. I think one of the finest things I have ever seen done since I have been in this House of Commons was when the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) spoke up as he did
630	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Sinclair and paid the brave tribute that he did to Donald Gordon. If people who are trying in their own spheres to do their job and hold the line against inflation-and it is a very difficult problem we have today-are to be abused and blackguarded in this House of Commons where they have no right of redress or reply, then I do not think we are going to find it so easy to get other people to come down here, the skilled and technical people we need to administer price control, as we did in the last war.
Then there is the third necessity for effective price control, and it is probably the most important of all. We may have legislation, good legislation modelled on that of the last war; we may have those skilled administrators; but unless we have public acceptance in Canada of the need and the urgency, then the program is doomed to failure before it even starts.
At times the Canadian people have been accused-especially by some of, our journalists who write learned magazine articles- of being people without much colour or imagination. However, there is one characteristic about the Canadian people. They will not be pushed around needlessly. There is no sacrifice that the Canadian people will not make for their country once they are convinced of the necessity of it. But a Canadian has an instinctive abhorrence and revulsion against unnecessary regimentation, unnecessary pushing around. One reason we were successful in the war was that the Canadian people knew these controls were imperative and that they were getting a fair break. We were all in that war together. I can tell you that from my own personal observation we were much more successful in complete public acceptance of these controls than either Great Britain or the United States, because we had, for example, very little in the way of black-marketing. It was the patriotic thing and the right thing to do to obey the law; no Canadian thought it smart to chisel. But today I have not noticed very much public acceptance of the fact that, with goods, though fairly high in price, still not in short supply, an over-all policy of clamping down controls, including, as it must, wage controls, is necessary.
Something has been said about the cost of living index standing at 168. Let us look at that for a moment. The 168 is based on what? It is based on the average cost of living between 1935 and 1939. Let us remember the conditions in 1935 and in 1939. In 1935 we had the worst unemployment the country had ever known. Even by 1939, according to a royal commission, 17 per cent of our working force were without jobs.

The Budget-Mr. Sinclair men over there, the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Jones) and the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) who have had more experience with instalment buying than all the others have had, who know its faults and advantages, but those members did not speak.
What has the government done thus far to check inflation? I cannot do better than turn to the report of the royal commission on price spreads and recall what they said should be done, and then to point out what the government has done.
First of all, the government can levy high taxes, leaving less and less for the people to spend. We have done that. We should take more money from the taxpayer today according to the hon, member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) although the policy was "mulcting the people" two years ago. We have certainly done that, and we are doing it again to meet our requirements.
Then there is the recommendation that we should discourage borrowing and the raising of capital for investment. Well, of course, with our curbs on consumer buying, housing loans and farm improvement loans, we are taking a step in that direction.
It is said that we should encourage savings. We did that in the last war by the issue of victory bonds, and, because the people of Canada thus got the habit for thrift, have continued since the war with dominion savings bonds.
Then, there is the recommendation to defer capital expenditures, and we will do that despite the hon. member for Queens (Mr. McLure) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who think that their projects in Winnipeg and in Queens should be gone ahead with, and economies made in other ridings.
Then the final recommendation of an overall control of prices and wages. I say that when the time comes for that it will be done as it was done during the war.
I was in the library reading up a 1939 Hansard which is in great demand at the present time and I was interested in the speech made by the Hon. H. H. Stevens, who was the financial critic at that time. He made a very able and clever speech and he said that he hoped the government would profit by the experiences gained in the 1914 war. Of course Canada in 1914 had never waged war. We went into the thing green and the government made some very bad mistakes and there were a number of scandals. Of course the 1939 government could and did profit by studying that record.
We came out of this war with a great record. The people of Canada were proud


of the war effort, of their industrial and agricultural production. Today we are in a still different position. In 1939 we did not have a great industrial potential, but during the war and in the last four years there has been tremendous industrial expansion in Canada and so we are that much better prepared. Then as an added asset we have in this parliament today key men in this government who were key men in the tremendous war effort that was made, who have not no knowledge of war demands as in 1914, or academic knowledge as in 1939, but practical knowledge because they ran our last war effort.
First and foremost is the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), who was then minister of justice. Then we have our own minister, who served under Mr. Ilsley and handled the wartime prices and trade board work. During that period we improved our food production tremendously to help our allies and that was done under the great leadership of the indomitable little Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner).
Then finally one last great asset. This morning on my way to the library I met a prominent Conservative businessman, at one time a Conservative member of parliament. He said to me, "I am glad that parliament passed that bill of Mr. Howe's last night. Both business and the people of Canada have tremendous faith in Mr. Howe because of what he has done." With this combination we can face the future with hope.

Then the hon. member went on to say that the tremendous cost of new plant and equipment which had been built in this country during the war was one of the factors which increased present prices. I agree with him. If the figures given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) are correct, and I believe they are, during the war there was built in this country between $4,000 million and $5,000 million worth of new plants and equipment.
Every bit of that plant and equipment was paid for by the people. Any person who has read the contracts that were made to cover the production of war materials knows that they contained clauses whereby a sufficient price was paid for the material purchased to cover the cost of plant and equipment. This was allowed by way of special depreciation. The result is that all that new plant and equipment is entirely paid for, paid for by the people of Canada through taxes and loans made to the government. All that new plant and equipment, however, is owned by private interests.
Everything which has been produced since that time by that plant and equipment has carried a price which has enabled the private interests to get what they say is a fair return on their plant and equipment which in fact was paid for by the people of Canada. The men who went overseas and who tried to establish themselves when they returned have had to pay prices which enabled the private interests to obtain a return which they considered to be fair on the plant and equipment paid for by the people of Canada. As the hon. member for Coast-Capilano has stated, that is one reason for the high cost of living. I agree with him.
Then the hon. member for Coast-Capilano said that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) had not answered the
The Budget-Mr. Wright hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Sinnott), who inquired with regard to our policy on wages. The hon. member for Coast-Capilano quoted part of what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said, but he did not quote this, and I quote from page 452 of Hansard of September 8, 1950:
I suggest that the government should call together the producers of this country, whether farm producers or wage earners, and discuss with them the levels which they feel would be reasonable and proper for both farm production and wages.
In other words, domestic wage and price control. We do not believe in freezing wages or farm prices at levels which are unduly unfair to the wage earners or primary producers. We do believe in wage control. We do believe in farm price control. That is the only way in a civilized economy in which you can get equity between various sections of the country.

-if you are going to make a statement you should be ready to back it up with facts. I want to pay a compliment to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I believe he is the only minister who has dealt realistically at this session with the facts in connection with matters which have affected his department. He has placed before this house a measure which recognizes the seriousness of the situation which exists today in the world. He has asked for power to impose the controls he believes may be necessary. Whether or not he is to use them, he has taken them so that if an emergency arises he can use them to do what should be done to meet the situation that exists in the world today. Let us read what the genial Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) had to say, as recorded at page 422 of Hansard. He said:
The increased defence expenditures being thrust heavily upon every country by these new manifestations of Russian imperialism, now open and unmasked, call for sound economic policies; and it is the duty of every country to deal promptly and effectively with the inflationary pressures generated within its own jurisdiction.

The Budget-Mr. Wright
He recognizes that inflationary pressures exist and will continue to exist. What is the position of the world today? Is the Korean situation just an incident, something that will be over in six or seven months? From my reading of the history of the past few years, I cannot be that optimistic. I think it is just another incident in a long train of events. If we are to deal effectively with that train of events it is going to be necessary to be prepared to deal with more than merely the Korean incident. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) has told us that if we are to have peace in the world the democracies must show strength. We have heard that from the state department of the United States. We have heard it from the minister of war of Great Britain. We have heard it from practically every country that is at present in the North Atlantic pact.
What strength is opposing us? According to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and other military experts, Russia has some 175 divisions mobilized today. Last June the democracies had some twenty divisions mobilized. If we are to use strength as a means to peace, let us not think for one moment that the Korean incident is going to be the only one, or that by stopping that aggression we are going to secure effective peace in Canada. If I am any judge of the position in the world today, we are going to be engaged for the next ten or twenty years in strengthening our democracies both militarily and economically to meet any threat in the world. If we are going to do that effectively, then in my opinion we have to adopt the necessary controls and make the necessary sacrifices to do it.
Under the present budget I cannot see that sacrifices are being made by the people of Canada to any extent to meet the situation existing in the world today. At page 421 of Hansard the Minister of Finance, in defending his position against controls, stated:
Finally I would say, without detracting in any way from the magnificent wartime job done by Mr. Donald Gordon and his associates, that the success of the wartime prices and trade board would have been impossible without three things-
I want hon. members to mark these three things.
First, the fact that we pursued a vigorous antiinflationary policy of maximum possible taxation supported by intensive savings campaigns;-
If the situation in the world today is serious, why does the government not follow that policy?

I do not want to deal further with this subject, but I would like to refer to the statement made in the house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce concerning the prices to be paid and the spreads between the grades of wheat. The minister indicated that in all probability this year we would have some 23 million bushels of No. 1 wheat, 55 million bushels of No. 2 wheat, 99 million bushels of No. 3 wheat, and 184 million bushels of No. 4 and lower grades. That is a total of some 361 million bushels, of which approximately 49 per cent will be No. 4 or lower. The minister also gave the spreads between the grades, and I think those spreads are quite realistic, considering the amount of low grade wheat that will have to be sold during the coming crop year. The fact that these spreads may be realistic, however, does not alter the further fact that it is going to mean a tremendous drop in the purchasing power of the wheat producers of western Canada. I have done some figuring on those spreads. Last year the initial payment on No. 1 wheat at Winnipeg was $1.75; this year it is to be $1.40. Last year the initial payment on No. 2 wheat was $1.72; this year it is to be $1.40, the same as for No. 1. From there on down, however, the spreads widen. Last year the initial payment for No. 3 wheat at Fort William and Port Arthur was $1.70; this year it is to be $1.30. For No. 4 Wheat last year the initial payment was $1.65 at Port Arthur; this year it is to be $1.22. For No. 5 it was $1.55; now it is to be $1.12. For No. 6 it was $1.51; now it is to be $1.06. Feed wheat was $1.49 last year; this year it is to be $1. In other words the spreads in the lower grades have widened so that this year there will be a considerably lower price paid for those lower grades as compared with last year.
As I said, I believe that these spreads are realistic, in view of the quantities of these lower grades that will have to be sold. However, it means that as far as the western farmer is concerned the average price he will receive for the wheat he has to sell, because of the lower grades and the greater spreads, will be approximately 25 cents a bushel less than last year. The initial payment will be 35 cents less, which means a drop of 60 cents a bushel in the initial payment he will receive when he delivers his crop this fall. A difference of 60 cents a bushel on


361 million bushels means a drop in purchasing power of approximately $216 million as compared with last year. Then last year the western farmer also received payments on past deliveries. I have before me the report of the wheat board for 1948-49, which states: During the crop year 1948-49 the payment division was concerned with the 20 cent adjustment payment authorized on wheat delivered to the board between August 1, 1945, and March 31, 1949, as well as in connection with previously authorized payments. During 1948-49 the payment division issued 1,365,559 cheques to producers with a value of $220,681,269.95.
So we have a decrease in the initial payment of $216 million. We have only one other payment due, which I shall deal with later. We also have a drop of $220 million in receipts on certificates, which means a total drop of some $436 million in the amount of money available to western farmers to purchase goods and services this fall.
