When the house rose at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was indicating to it the cash position of the western grain growers with respect to this year's crop, owing to the severe frost which occurred in western Canada and owing to the reduced prices and reduced grades this year. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) had interrupted me to point out that it was estimated that the deliveries this year were going to be larger than those of last year. I had pointed out to him that at the present time I am giving the deficit side of the picture and that I would later give the credit side and show the balance in losses to western agriculture as a result of the present prices and the present condition of the crop in western Canada. I had pointed out the difference between the prices at Fort William as compared with last year; and I should like to give the average price which the farmer

receives in western Canada, as represented by the figures showing the price of the various grades of grain at Regina which is a twenty-cent freight rate point in western Canada, and represents about the average price which the farmer would receive.
At Regina this year the farmer will receive $1.23J for No. 1 wheat as compared with $1.57J last year. But as I pointed out before, most of the crop this year will be No. 4 or lower, according to the figures given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce this morning. No. 4 wheat is selling at $1.05J as compared with $1.48J last year while feed wheat is selling at 83J cents this year as compared with $1.32J last year.
As I have stated, this represents a loss in purchasing power, when taken along with the payments which were made last year, of some $436 million less cash in the hands of western grain producers. That is just the wheat picture.
If we take barley, we find that last year most of the western crop was of an extremely fine quality and graded malting barley, and was mostly sold at $1.40 a bushel or over. As a matter of fact, in a letter from my own farm received today I note that, whereas last year our barley averaged 40 bushels to the acre and sold at No. 2 C. W. this year it is going at No. 2 feed and will sell at less than 70 cents a bushel, or just about half. There will therefore be a loss in coarse grains of approximately $50 million as compared with last year.
Then last year in western Canada there was a part of an area in Saskatchewan and Alberta in which P.F.A.A. payments were made. There was a crop failure in that area and $22 million was paid under P.F.A.A. to the farmers there. This year very little will be paid under prairie farm assistance, even though the value of the crop may be quite low. As hon. members know, prairie farm assistance is paid on the basis of the number of bushels grown. If the average number of bushels in any given township is over eight to the acre, there is no P.F.A.A. payment. This year there will be little in the way of payments under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
If you add together those figures that I have given it will be found that there will be in the hands of the western farmers this year approximately $508 million less purchasing power on the basis of the initial payment this year and the initial payment last year and the other factors I have mentioned. I can therefore assure the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that, as far as the western agriculturalist is concerned, there is not going to be a great deal of pressure on his price
The Budget-Mr. Wright ceiling when it comes to purchasing the various needs of the agriculturalists in western Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The inflationary pressure is not going to be as great this year?

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As the Minister of Trade and Commerce has stated, there is an increased production this year. Last year there were delivered to the wheat board approximately 318 million bushels. This year it is estimated that 361 million bushels will be delivered, or approximately 40 million bushels more. At $1.05 a bushel, that amounts to approximately $45 million.
Then there is also whatever payment the government may intend to make on the five-year pool. According to the wheat board reports which I have here in my hand it is quite evident, from the figures that are given in it, that from 5 cents to 6 cents would be the amount that is left in the pool for payment. If it were 5 cents, there are approximately 1,400 million bushels of wheat on which that amount will be paid, which would mean approximately $70 million. We therefore have $101 million to put over against the figure of $508 million or, in round figures, approximately $400 million less purchasing power in the hands of western agriculturists this year as compared with last year.
I think those figures should indicate to the government that they should do one of two things. They should see that the final payment on the five-year pool is substantially larger than the amount indicated as being in the pool, and they should see that the initial price paid on this year's crop is increased. The initial price indicated by the government is $1.40 per bushel. The government should act on these suggestions or they should see that the things the farmer has to buy in order to produce this crop are held at a reasonable price level and in fair relationship to his prices.
Anyone who wants to do a bit of figuring can compare the cost today of the things the farmer has to buy and that in the 1935-39 period. The cost index today is approximately 200. It was 196 according to the last figure I saw, and it has been increasing since then. In other words, it costs twice as much for the farmer to produce a bushel of wheat today as it did in the 1985-39 period. According to these figures, however, the average price we are going to receive for that wheat this year is $1.05 per bushel. It therefore does not take much figuring to see that in purchasing power that $1.05 today equals only 60 cents in 1939. Therefore the western producers of grain are back this year to the position they were in in 1939.

The Budget-Mr. Wright
The minister asked me if I thought the farmers in my constituency believed that we should have controls. I would say certainly they believe we should have controls. The position they are in today is the result of the removal of controls. In 1944 and 1945, when we had controls in this country they were in a much better relative position with regard to purchasing power than they are today. Their position is becoming just a little worse all the time; over the last two years it has gradually become worse than it was in 1944 and 1945.
I would say that the report I read of the united farmers of Saskatchewan is a genuine opinion of the majority of the farmers in western Canada. They believe in an economy in which there is some fair relationship between the purchasing power of the farm product, the wages paid to labour and the returns to industry in this country. They have indicated that. They have indicated it by their support of the government's policy with respect to the wheat board; they have indicated it by the support of the international wheat agreement. They have indicated it on every occasion on which they have had the opportunity to show that they believed in an economy in which there are the necessary controls, because they know, as I stated before the dinner adjournment, that if the government removes controls somebody else takes them over, and that somebody else operates them not in the interest of the economy as a whole, but in the interest of his own particular sector of the economy. That is one of the major reasons why I am convinced that if we are to get a maximum effort to create conditions in this world which will produce in the democratic countries the results which will give them the strength that is needed in the world situation today, the only way in which we can do it is to be wise enough to adopt the necessary controls to get the maximum production in this country. I am sure of this: if you leave western agriculture in the position in which it finds itself today as the result of this year's crop, it will not be able to produce as efficiently as it should, and no other sector of the economy can produce unless it is in the position where it is in a fair relationship with the other sections of our economy. That is the policy of this group. We ask only for a fair relationship. We are not asking for regimentation; we are just asking for the imposition of controls that are necessary in a democratic economy to produce the best results for all of the people in that economy.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I refer to the main notes of my speech

I should like to pay tribute to the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) on what I believe to be one of the best speeches he has delivered. He has shown this house that he has knowledge; he has a clear brain, and be understands the working of his department. I think it is a tribute to his constituency to have such a man here to take care of their affairs.
We have heard the armchair and street-corner critics of our system of democracy and of this government complain that parliament moves too slowly, lacks efficiency and is incapable of speedy action. I think it can and should be said that, in addition to other important matters, this emergency session of the house has flatly proven that that is not so and given the lie to that sort of carping criticism. This government and this house have shown that since August 29, when parliament convened, it could move and has moved, with speed and efficiency equal to that of any government of any country.
It is true that we have had to sit three times a day, and that many of us have been hard pressed for time on that account; but I must say that these three sittings a day have advanced the business of the public at a time when it was so vital to move swiftly. In settling the matters of vital importance now before this house the government has cleared the way for the dominion-provincial conference and for the over-all plans for social security which we all trust will emerge from that most important conference.
There is not a single member of this house, I am sure, who does not deplore the fact that a nation-wide transportation system was tied up by the railway strike. Since management and labour both floundered on the rocks of disagreement, it was left to this House of Commons and this government to take action whereby trains again are on the move. In my opinion the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) and their colleagues-not forgetting the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier)-rendered a notable service to this country through the action which was taken in bringing the strike to an end, and paving the way for new negotiations between the railway unions and the railway management.
I was at a loss to understand the tactics of the opposition, which if followed would have settled nothing and which would have had the result only of prolonging this extremely grave situation and interruption of the economy of our country.

I am proud to join with other members in congratulations to our Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on the emergency budget which he submitted to this house last Thursday evening. In that budget he found means by which he could raise funds to meet Canada's obligations under the United Nations charter and the North Atlantic treaty with a minimum of interference with the productive capacity of this country.
We can truthfully say that all our constituents are both pleased and thankful that there was no increase in personal income tax in the budget which was recently brought down. Any increase in income tax would have met an understandable refusal of people to work overtime and hence work themselves into a higher tax bracket. You all remember world war II, when because of heavy taxation some workers declined offers to work overtime on the ground that they "would not work for Ilsley." This I am convinced certainly did curtail some production during world war II. I am sure that withholding an increase in personal income tax will mean increased production of all materials, when such materials are demanded.
Many people of course will deplore the fact that new taxes have been added to chocolate bars, candy, gum, soft drinks, beer, liquor, and other beverages, and while I say nothing against any of these items, I do not believe it will do any harm to any of us either to pay the additional tax or to cut down our consumption of the taxed items.
I believe most of the Canadian people will agree with the Minister of Finance in taxing corporations, increasing the rate of taxation from ten to fifteen per cent and from thirty-three to thirty-eight per cent.
Housewives across this country, and even more the brides and engaged couples, appreciate the consideration given by the Minister of Finance in exempting such household essentials as refrigerators, electric stoves and washing machines from additional taxes. Those items certainly are not a luxury and are needed in every home. These people can now go ahead with a minimum of disturbance in their plans for the future. We have heard appeals from the other side of the house for setting up of price controls such as we knew [DOT] during world war II, and we have heard reasons given by both the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) why these controls are not reimposed at this time.
I feel these reasons are sound, and more so because they are the considered opinion of
The Budget-Mr. Sinnott men who have had years of experience in administering price controls. They know the advantages and the faults of a controls system, and I am satisfied to be guided by their opinion-as, I am sure, are the Canadian people.
I asked the leader of the C.C.F. party on Friday, September 8, if his party was prepared to endorse controls of prices and wages and I received so long and vague a reply that it is clear that the socialist party in this House of Commons is not prepared to commit itself to an over-all system of price and wage control, but is following a wait and see policy.
This matter was referred to in the house just before the dinner adjournment. I should like to refer to page 452 of Hansard where I asked the following question of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), leader of the C.C.F. party:
I listened attentively to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, and I should like to ask one question. Does he propose that the government should impose over-all control on wages and prices?
The hon. member replied-and I am going to read all that he said, not just part of it:
I suggest that the government should call together the producers of this country, whether farm producers or wage earners, and discuss with them the levels which they feel would be reasonable and proper for both farm production and wages. During the war there was very little difficulty about the wage earners coming to an understanding and controlling their own wage levels. We were free from strikes and major dislocations. I notice that hon. gentlemen opposite share with us the view that if you can get something without compulsion it is better to do so, and I have no doubt that the unity of labour, in view of the necessity for preventing aggression at tile present time, would enable us to come to suitable arrangements with them for the voluntary control of the wage situation.
So far as industry and other factors in the economy are concerned, the situation is somewhat different. You cannot get together the thousands of people who are producing and distributing all sorts of things, in the same way that you can get the organized groups together, the organized farmers and the organized wage earners. However, in that way X think we could arrive at a decision which would be beneficial to the whole country.
Then I said:
Even after the question I asked and the lengthy answer of the hon. member X still do not understand whether or not he proposes over-all wage and price control.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What was the answer?

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I read the speech of the leader of the C.C.F. party from beginning to end, and I never found in any part of it whether he was in favour of wage and price controls. When he is asked the question he says, "I suggest that the government should call together the producers of this country." That

The Budget-Mr. Sinnott is not his policy; he is just suggesting it. But it is not the policy of his party. He is just suggesting it to the government, as political bait.
The policy of the official opposition on this matter of a price control system is even more vague than that of the C.C.F. The Tory party, that was hammering at the government all during the post-war years to remove controls faster and faster, now seems to be snuggling up to the price control theory, and when I saw just a few days ago the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) shaking hands with the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) just after he had finished speaking on controls, it made me wonder-what strange bedfellows. The very people who were dissatisfied with an orderly decontrol policy which the government followed from 1945 to 1950 are now clamouring for restoration of the very policy which they have been so violently opposing. We wonder what their supporters scattered around in a few parts of this country will think of this reversal of form. Or perhaps the leader of the opposition and his colleagues have finally decided to tear up that party's program-

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Again?

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-and give it the new look, the same as the C.C.F. has done from time to time.
The measures introduced during this emergency session and which we have been discussing are clear-cut, realistic and meet the needs of the very serious international situation which all of us are now called upon to face.
In the past, Mr. Speaker, I have never hesitated either on the floor of this house or in the councils of this party to oppose legislation in which I did not have confidence. I disagreed with a government policy on oil and gas plans and said so, until our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) gave us assurance that if it was at all possible to build the line within Canada, this would be done.
The interruptions and noises coming from hon. members opposite can be considered in the same light as they are given. If you tap an empty beer barrel, all you hear is a hollow sound.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The voice of experience.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I consider that the legislation announced in the speech from the throne, and presented to us in the various bills now before the chamber, is of a character that no right-thinking Canadian can oppose.
I recognize and respect honest differences of opinion, but it would be a shabby thing indeed if after binding ourselves to international agreements both under the United

Nations charter and under the North Atlantic treaty we reneged on these obligations.
The defence appropriation act deals with conditions as they are and the means to be taken to meet these conditions. Canada's name already enjoys a proud position through the operations of our destroyers in Korean waters and the flights of our planes on the Japan-Korea airlift, and if the government was seeking any endorsation of its policy in creating the Canadian Army special force, it certainly received it at recruiting offices from Newfoundland to Vancouver island. Strong, capable and patriotic young men flocked to those offices to take up arms in the defence of the freedom won for this country in the last two great wars. They are prepared to fight for that freedom in any country in the world where acts of aggression are committed. They realize also that while they are absent from Canada's shores it is essential that a highly skilled and trained force remain in this country to defend it against possible acts of aggression against our own territory; and all of us, I am sure, will support the government's action in strengthening our over-all national defences to meet the changed conditions and the deepening emergency that now confronts us.
While following the debates in the house for the past week I have found a curious lack of consistency in the criticism put forward by the official opposition. It sounded to me as if, rather than follow any fixed path of criticism, they followed the old slogan, "Every man for himself and devil take the hindmost".
We hear the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) striking out in one direction and the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) heading down the road to conscription. We hear the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) approving of Canadian military intervention in Korea and the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Courtemanche) walking down Isolation street. We see some members of the Conservative party taking halting steps towards price control and others remaining grimly silent.
We hear the clamour of the opposition for a committee on national defence composed of members from the whole house. What would the Canadian people think of their elected representatives to whom they have given trust to administer their affairs if they were to succumb to the clamouring of the opposition to take part in a committee of national defence and who would do their utmost to muddle the affairs of the government?

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They do not need any more muddling.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is only in the opinion of the empty beer barrel. In my opinion the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) is to be commended for his restraint against accusations of failing to give information when he is constantly giving all the information at his command. His very patience in the face of these rather absurd charges assures us that a cool head is directing the expansion of our defence forces, a head that will not be diverted by political baiting or stampeded into rash procedure.
In the course of this debate we have heard one or two members from the maritimes, and one I believe from my own province, urge a course of decentralization of manufacturing for war purposes. In an all-out war, I believe decentralization of war industry is very essential in the event of large-scale enemy air attack. Of course Canada is not mobilizing her industrial resources for an all-out war any more than she is mobilizing her manpower for that purpose. Hence it may well be that such requests made to the Minister of Trade and Commerce are premature. If, however, in the days to come it should be our misfortune to be forced into another total war [ would commend decentralization of war industry to the minister's attention. It can be said no man in Canada is as fully aware as he is of the location of this country's resources and the best means of developing them for either peace or war purposes.
In the province of Manitoba in world war [I we had a large explosive plant at the adge of my constituency at Transcona. This plant was second to none in its efficiency and productive capacity. Should circumstances ae such that similar plants will be required .n the future, I can assure the minister that ny province can provide the necessary hydroelectric power and also the men and women reeded for that operation.
I would not wish to take my seat without paying tribute to the Prime Minister. No man .n Canada has worked harder or as unselfishly ,n the interests of the Canadian people. When ;he last session came to an end most of us rad an opportunity for a holiday or if not a roliday at least a change of scene and a :hange of work. It has been his misfortune ;hat when a vacation was most needed he was lalled time after time to Ottawa from his summer home. Finally he had to abandon altogether the idea of a few days' well-earned relaxation. On his shoulders fell the final lecision in the railway strike and the final lecision of calling parliament back to meet the Korean situation. Those two delicate lecisions were of the most difficult and complex nature. I believe, and Canadians in general believe, that he not only reached the best possible decision in both cases but recon-
The Budget-Mr. Hansell ciled conflicting opinions so as to advance the great cause of national unity in this country.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I once read a rather interesting article which stated that you can always determine the spirit of the age by the phraseology it uses.
I do not now refer to the speech of the hon. member who has preceded me, but I do refer to some of the phraseology used by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) when he brought down his chocolate bar-pop bottle budget the other night. I fancied I could detect the spirit of government policy in the phraseology used. It is possible to becloud important issues by charming phraseology but to more keen-minded students phraseology is nothing but a dead giveaway.
In reading over the minister's speech and after listening to him the other night I find that there are one or two phrases I should like to comment upon briefly. I trust that, pointing out these phrases and using them as a basis for what I say, will not be considered as a weak argument. The minister talked of . the necessity of maintaining peace by force. A phrase of that kind or similar phrases have been used over and over again this session. When one analyses that phrase he finds that it just does not mean a thing unless it means war.
It is impossible to maintain peace by force. Force is an element of warfare. The only basis for proper peace is the contentment of nations, and you cannot force contentment. When you are dealing with peace and war you are not dealing with materialistic principles, you are dealing with certain life principles and life principles cannot be forced. I hope the minister will follow my philosophy. It is just the same as a husband using a club on his wife in an attempt to beat her into loving him. You just cannot do that; it just will not work. Perhaps some hon. members have tried it. If they have, I am sure they have met with sad disappointment. Contentment of nations and the peace of heart and mind among nations cannot be maintained by force.
Another phrase used by the minister was that there has been "a new manifestation of Russian imperialism, now open and unmasked." Surely the minister did not mean that when he said it. If he did then he exposes himself to one of the greatest weaknesses of which any public man has ever been guilty. Surely the minister does not mean that the outbreak of the skirmish in Korea is the new manifestation of Russian imperialism, and that now it is open and unmasked. Surely he has known that for a good many years. Any student of Marx, Lenin, Engels

The Budget-Mr. Hansell and communist world strategy knows that there is no new manifestation, that it has not been recently opened and unmasked.
Before the war and throughout the war years we in this corner of the house stood up time and time again to warn of the dangers of communist aggression in the world. Over and over again we stood in this corner of the house and warned about the communist fronts that were being set up in Canada and elsewhere throughout the free democratic world. We warned over and over again of thesa things. Surely no one in such a responsible position as that now held by the Minister of Finance could possibly have been misled. Yet we find that some of the great men of the earth were inveigled into certain positions, perhaps by force of circumstances-I do not know-where they made mistakes and pursued certain policies that have brought us to the present dilemma.
I was reading the other day about an incident that happened in England. The leader of a certain communist front known as the European liberation front, Anthony Gannon, stood up and reminded Mr. Churchill of some of the things he had said about Russia during the war. It may be an alarming thing for us to review some of the phraseology that Mr. Churchill used then.
, Here is what he said: "God bless you, Stalin." "Stalin the great." "This great rugged war chief" "My heart bleeds for Russia." "Their word is their bond." These are not the words of communists. They are none other than the words of Mr. Winston Churchill in days gone by. It is a startling thing, is it not, that some of the greatest leaders of the nations should say such things in times of crisis knowing full well that the day would come when communist aggression would have to be dealt with by the free nations of the world. The communists have to remind us of what we said; a sad, sad picture, indeed.
Therefore I say to the minister: Whom does he think he is fooling when he says that this new manifestation of Russian imperialism is now open and unmasked?
There is another phrase that he used. It has been mentioned before during the past few days. I think it is a phrase that contains perhaps the crux of the discussions that have taken place throughout this special session of parliament. The minister said, "of course we are not in a state of war but at a hill of difficulty on the path of peace". Once again I should like to ask him whom he thinks he is kidding. It is a nice thing to say that in order to get around some sort of little technicality. We do not want to declare


a war, it would be dangerous to do so, but we will mobilize a force and send it to the war front to stop communist aggression.
It is all very well to put together phrases that will let the people of the country down easy. Therefore the minister says that we are not in a state of war but at a hill of difficulty on the path to peace. I do not think these verbal gymnastics fool anyone. Just ask the United States soldiers in Korea whether or not we are at war. When the 10,000 or 15,000 Canadian troops get over there, just ask them whether or not we are at war. I know that a verbal battle has been going on between the opposition, particularly our Conservative friends, and the government as to whether or not the government should declare a state of emergency. The government have said that they will not declare a state of emergency because if they did so it would of course indicate that we are at war. So what happens? They like to say that we are not at war, that we are marching over a difficult hill toward peace, but we will send our troops over there to slug it out with the enemy. It just does not add up.
If I may, I should like to give the house my own analysis and diagnosis of the situation. As I see it, this is the picture, and it is based partially on the fact that we now have a wartime budget of some $3,400 million, including in round figures a billion dollars for defence alone. Is anyone going to say that it takes that much money simply to send 10,000 or 15,000 troops to Korea? We have been debating a bill that puts unlimited controls into the hands of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). Will anyone say for a moment it is necessary to do that in order to send a mere ten or fifteen thousand troops to Korea? And why have we voted certain commitments to meet certain possible eventualities?
As I see it, Mr. Speaker, the picture is something like this: When the government decided1 to send some troops to Korea, in view of the promise by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) that no troops would be sent unless parliament was called, naturally the government had to call parliament. They had to decide whether the people of Canada would accept a wartime economy for the purpose of backing up the efforts of the United Nations. In other words they had to decide whether or not the people had sufficient confidence in the United Nations to accept the internal position of a nation at war. That was what they had to decide. The other day the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) was very determined in stating that the great principle at stake was not confined to Korea, that we were

fighting a great world struggle. If my notes are correct he said, "It is a great principle that free nations will unite to preserve their freedom." In another place he said^ "It has to be a free system or a slave system." I think the Minister of Finance will agree with those statements. But now I ask: is that great struggle between the free nations and those other great forces which would impose upon the world a system of slavery confined to what I would describe as a sort of sideshow now going on in Korea? The answer, to my mind, is easy to find. My personal opinion is that the legislation we have been called upon to pass this session, together with the budget of the Minister of Finance, constitutes the initial step in preparation for what in future may become a world struggle. It seems to me that to say anything less is to understate the possibilities.
Now I should like to go on to deal with another matter which I feel should be raised again. I am not going to criticize this budget too harshly; in fact I think the minister has shown a good deal of common sense in bringing down such a budget at this time. I will say, however, that members of parliament may as well get themselves set for their return next January, because unless things change in the world we are going to be given much harsher budgets than this. Of course, as I have said before, whether the people are prepared to stand for the internal economy of the country being placed upon a wartime footing is something we may doubt at the present time. The Korean struggle, what I called a sideshow, has not come home to us too forcibly as yet.
It has been said over and over again in. this house that the cost of living is going up. I am not going to particularly labour that point; we all know it. We in this corner of the house have proposed over and over again a monetary policy that we believe would manage the country's economy so that prices would not rise unduly; but I say that where prices rise as the direct action of profiteers, then those profiteers should be punished severely. When the railway strike was on a little while ago some industries in Canada took advantage of that strike and deliberately raised consumer prices, in spite of the fact that there was no shortage of the commodities with which they dealt. That can .be done also when a national crisis comes upon us, such as a period of conflict.
Some time ago I was reading an article by a United States economist dealing with the inflation of the United States dollar. I cannot say just where I read this; I do not have 69262-Hi
The Budget-Mr. Hansell time to mark and file everything away. We are not given sufficient help to permit us to do that sort of thing, so we must trust to our memory. In any case, this economist said that if the inflation of the American dollar continued as it had gone on since the pre-war years, by 1999, or at the turn of the century, the American dollar would be worth less than five cents. I do not know what the United States government is going to do about it. If that is the case a suit of clothes which now sells for $50, at the turn of the century will cost $1,000. A shirt that may cost $5 today will cost $100. We may say "oh, well, in fifty years we will not be here". Reduce the period to ten years; at the present rate that suit of clothes will be worth $200, while the shirt will be worth $20.
That is a problem for the United States, but I might come a little closer home. The other day we picked up the Ottawa Citizen and read how a reporter had dug up some rather interesting information from an old Citizen some considerable number of years ago. The item was from the Citizen of 1879. That is just seventy years ago. I think perhaps all hon. members read that article. He said that shirts were selling at 75 cents and coats were selling at $4.25. If you figure that out properly at today's prices and note the inflation that has gradually taken place over the years, right here in Canada at the turn of the century we shall be paying $410 for a suit of clothes and $132 for a shirt.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You will not have even a shirt.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That-is all right. Keep your shirt on. Even in ten years' time we shall be paying $130 to $140 for a suit of clothes; that is, at the rate of inflation since 1879. The strange thing to me is this, and here is where I blame the fiscal or monetary policy of the government. With the advent of the power machine, when machines take labour off the backs of our workers and should produce goods much more cheaply than hand labour would produce them many years ago, we have to pay a tremendous amount more for the products of these machines. Will you tell me why that is so? Physically, there is no answer to it; it cannot be answered. It can only be answered in terms of government monetary policy.
I wish to say one other thing, Mr. Speaker, and then I shall be through. I do not know how the present crisis which this nation is facing and the present policy of the Minister of Finance is going to affect that which we have all been looking forward to. I refer now to the social security legislation which

The Budget-Mr. Hansell this house has been working on and expecting for some considerable time. We have already been told in the last session of this house that it would cost in the neighbourhood of half a billion dollars to put into operation a sufficient or, shall I say, partially-sufiicient old age pension scheme. I hope that in the present crisis we have not lost sight of that objective. Should the Minister of Finance reply or should the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) speak in this present debate, I believe he should give us some information as to whether we can expect the government to continue to pursue their proposed policy with regard to bringing in proper social security legislation. Is this social security legislation now at a standstill or can we hope to see it introduced in the not too distant future?
Once again right here I want to say a word for our friends, the many incurable people in Canada. The minister is aware of their plight, as we all are. I am sure the minister himself will recognize the fact that their need is even greater than the need of the old age pensioners, great as their need is. I do not know whether we can hold out a great deal of hope for those unfortunate people. I urge that at the earliest possible moment this present administration consult with the provincial administrations and determine right soon that they are going to do something for these unfortunate people.
I do not know what is on the entire agenda for the forthcoming dominion-provincial conference. Perhaps a good deal of time will be taken in trying to unravel and to agree on some constitutional .changes. I do not know whether our incurables are greatly concerned with the constitutional exactitudes that these governments may be fighting about, but I say this: If the government has any responsibility at all, surely it has a responsibility to those who find it impossible even to help themselves. I again urge them to place on their agenda for the forthcoming conference the plight of the incurables in Canada. If that is impossible, and if they cannot place that subject on their agenda for this coming conference, I urge them to bring down, not later than next session, legislation that will give these poor unfortunate people at least a break.
Over and over again, Mr. Speaker, we have said that there is a great deal of money for war but no money for these great needs in time of peace. Are we going to repeat that mistake? Surely not. Surely we have proved that this nation is able to make the necessary provision if only the government is willing to bring down legislation that will benefit those who cannot possibly help themselves.
[Mr. Hansell.)

I do not think I have any more to say at the present moment, Mr. Speaker. I am not going to be harshly critical of the minister's budget. I feel that within his budget there is an element of strategy; which is to let the people down easy for a while; we will sort of creep up on them; but eventually, of course, if a great struggle develops between the two great forces, one of which is clamouring for world power and the other for its survival, the going will indeed be tough.
I hardly know how we can visualize the future if we think of it in terms of a great world struggle. We hope it does not come. We hope that government policy-here, in Great Britain, and the United States-will be such that we shall be able to avert this possible tragedy between these two great forces. We hope it can be averted. Let us pray that Divine Providence will prevent it. Let us one and all do our best and, putting politics aside, let us do all we can to preserve the peace among men.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a freshman member of this house I could not be expected to answer the force of the speech delivered earlier by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Sinnott), nor the eloquence of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell). If I do not attempt to answer either of them I trust it will not be taken as an indication that I subscribe to the arguments which may have been advanced. As a matter of fact, if I heard the hon. member for Springfield correctly, I think he in a moment of exuberance referred to one of the outstanding teetotallers in this House of Commons as "an empty beer barrel". Possibly the soundness of his arguments may be gauged from that. I also noticed that he inferentially, at any rate, criticized the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) for having spoken to, associated with or shaken hands with the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). I do not need to assure you, sir, or certainly any of the people of the province from which I come, that the hon. member for Cape Breton South is recognized as one of the spokesmen of the maritime provinces. Possibly the stature to which he has attained is due in no small part to the fact that he has uttered sentiments and1 voiced desires which should have been better expressed by hon. members on the government side of this house.
Without subscribing entirely to the sentiments expressed by the last speaker I am sure that we all, recognizing the financial problems of the moment, echo his desire that everything possible be done for that class of people to whom he referred in the latter part of his speech. I am sure that all of us have

received letters daily from hopelessly crippled and incurable people who present pathetically pleas which wring the heart of every hon. member. We hope and trust that sometime in the near future, if not now, this government will be able to advance measures which will be of assistance to that class of people.
I do agree with him that there is somewhat of an atmosphere of unreality about this debate and about the budget. During the last few days, as I have sat here and watched the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and recalled the days in which we were associated in great undertakings when we together shared certain responsibilities and certain risks, I thought of the question that we then rhetorically asked: "Daddy, what did you do in the great war?" We thought then that the greatest and the highest answer which could be given was to say: "I served in the artillery".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This time I suspect that the generations coming up will be asked by their daddies: "Son, what did you do in the third war or the Korean war", or call it what you will, and they will say: "Daddy, 1 paid ten cents for a chocolate bar". That seems to me to be the measure of the-

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I heard the remarks from
the other side, but I do suggest this, sir, however lightly they may be taken: there are some who question the wisdom of taxing the chocolate bars which are associated with our children's lives in this country today. The taxes on chocolate bars and soft drinks have been increased thirty per cent whereas spirits have been increased ten per cent. I think that is part of the atmosphere of unreality to which reference could be made at this time.
We have had a great picture of a buoyant economy. The Minister of Finance, I think with some justification, has pointed out the fact that we have had a prosperity almost greater than ever before. He said that there is great employment, high wages and a buoyant income throughout the Country. So great is it that yesterday we were forced to deal with legislation restricting credit purchases of people, many of whom, I suggest sir, are not in particularly affluent circumstances. That may be, and undoubtedly is, one way in which to deal with the pressures which we see rising around us.
Like the hon. member who last spoke, I have not a filing system and I do not remember just where I saw it, and the figures may
The Budget-Mr. Nowlan be inaccurate, but I know I took it from an editorial which appeared within the last few days in one of our national papers. It said that the wages paid by this government in 1949 were $313 million; whereas the wages which were paid in 1939, ten years before, were but $77 million. There, sir, you see inflationary pressure. I suggest this is a matter in which economies could be effected and inflationary pressures reduced.
Dealing with buoyant economy, I also noticed in the press yesterday that the dairy farmers of Canada received in June, 1950, over $3,500,000 less than they received in June, 1949. There is no great buoyant economy there, sir. I wonder how much their costs have increased over June, 1949. I know naught about the dairy industry of central Canada, but I do know of it in the east. I know that those people in the extreme distances of this dominion pay a higher cost for freight and the rest of it, and are farther away from markets than the other sections of the country, and they are faced continually with the pressure of increasing costs and decreasing returns. These things are threatening that industry to such an extent that many of those now engaged in it may be forced out of it in the very near future. If that happens I do not have to suggest to anyone here what the effect will be upon the dairy industry of Canada as a whole.
Tonight I am not going to discuss general matters. I want to refer to one particular matter, namely, the situation that in my judgment exists in or applies to eastern Canada, and particularly to Nova Scotia and my own constituency. It is undoubtedly true that in many places in Canada there is a buoyant economy. It is undoubtedly true that because of increased government expenditures, because of expenditures which are going to flow necessarily from wartime production, money will increase in central Canada and in other places throughout Canada. But, sir, I am suggesting to you that in the east we are not going to benefit from this wartime or so-called wartime expenditure.
The situation is entirely different from what it was in the years that followed after 1939 when great convoys of ships sailed from the eastern Canadian seaboard, and when one could drive over the roads in my own province and see 200, 300 ships in convoy lying in "an eastern Canadian seaport" waiting to sail for overseas, and the shipyards and the dockyards and every other industry in eastern Canada were working day and night in order to keep those ships equipped and supplied with provisions. Those days are not going to return during the

The Budget-Mr. Nowlan crisis while we surmount this hill ot emergency to which the minister referred the other night.
We are going to have to bear our part of the costs. We are not going to receive from these wartime expenditures any corresponding benefit whatsoever, if one wishes to call it a benefit. I am thinking particularly now of an industry in my own constituency, namely, the apple industry which has existed in the Annapolis valley for over a century, which but a few years ago was the largest within the British empire, and which even up to the outbreak of the last war exported more apples than did any other fruit-growing district in the entire British commonwealth. What is the condition there today? Once there was an outbreak of war, that industry became a wartime casualty. The government recognized that fact and dealt with it in many ways, and on the whole in a fair and adequate manner.
Then came the end of the war. It was hoped that the industry could be re-established. But what followed? Owing to the exchange situation and the dollar problem that industry is once more deprived of the markets which were its traditional heritage, and practically its only outlet. So that today the growers in the valley are facing a situation wherein, owing to increased freight rates, they are prohibited from delivering to other parts of Canada, and because of exchange controls they are prohibited from exporting outside of Canada. The result is that we are now restricted to that small market in the maritime provinces, with some slight access perhaps to the market in eastern Quebec and in the city of Montreal.
The growers there tonight, sir, are facing a very grim situation indeed. The crop is on the trees. To pick or not to pick is the question. If they pick, then who supplies the cost? Who supplies the labour cost of picking, the cost of containers, the cost of storage? If they do not pick, then the crop is destined to freeze on the trees within the next few days or, at the outside, within the next few weeks. As I said, only a proportion of the crop can be sold locally. It is a decision the growers have to make-and I suggest it is a decision concerning which they should receive some assistance and some direction from the government of this country.
I am not for one moment saying that critically. All of us who have been here in the last three weeks realize the pressure which has been borne by all members- a pressure which, may I say in parentheses, I hope will not be experienced again in any future session of parliament, because members of parliament cannot do their duty working under such


pressure as this. And if there has been pressure on the ordinary member, I realize just how much greater must be the pressure upon the ministers, the members of the government.
I do say however that some decision must be made, and that some decision must be made soon. Last year the Minister of Agriculture (Mr Gardiner) said, in response to a question in the house, that the fruit-growing industry was entitled to price support. I think that is a matter which is established by legislation by the law of this country. We need to know soon, in the east, what lead is to be given, in order that a decision may be made as to whether all of this crop is, or is not, going to be harvested.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) has emphasized on various occasions the necessity for and the importance of exporting goods to those countries more depressed than our own. I believe we all subscribe to that view. We all realize that, go over the hills of difficulty as we may, we will not defeat communism nor will we eradicate it by battalions or by bayonets. This can only be done by improving the living standards and living conditions throughout the world.
The export of food is one way-perhaps a small way-in which that can be done. In the area to which I have been referring there will be within the next few weeks hundreds of thousands, perhaps millions of dollars worth of food which may be lost. My suggestion is that action should be taken whereby a substantial portion of that which heretofore we have exported to Great Britain might be processed, put into cans and shipped overseas-if necessary it should be shipped to those depressed areas, and given away, where communism is now rampant. Because I can assure the house that communism does not thrive on full stomachs-and particularly if one has his stomach full of apple pie composed of Nova Scotia canned apples. Certainly that would be true if the apple pies were anything like the ones made in my home.
I do not want to enter into a discussion of local problems. I realize the danger of engaging in a discussion of local issues, and the possibility of starting a sort of chain reaction throughout the house. It is not my wish to do that at all. But I have attempted in discussing this matter affecting my own district to speak not only for the farmers there but for those in the east, generally. We are prepared now to pay, and in the past have paid our full cost to build and maintain this Dominion of Canada, and those costs have borne heavily upon us.
