speechtext: Ontario and Quebec.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Ontario and Quebec-your central waterways, and all the rest of it. There are costs, and they will not be insignificant, lying ahead of us. But I do suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott)- and I know he appreciates the situation-that if he is going to maintain the balanced economy throughout this country that is so essential, if he is going to fight in depressed areas, and if he is going to have the people loyally working behind him, climbing these hills to which he referred the other night- because there is more than one hill on the way-then he must build up the economy of the country so that those in the east who did not benefit at all from defence or wartime expenditures may receive money in some other way. One of those ways-and I know the Minister of Agriculture recognizes this fact-one of the important ways in which this must be done is to assist the agricultural industry in the east along lines I have suggested tonight, and in other ways which I could suggest if I were so inclined.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to thank the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) for coming to my rescue.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You don't need much rescuing.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I did not think it was such a great crime for the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) to shake hands with me. We do that quite often, and I hope the time will never come in the House of Commons when, despite differences of opinion on political matters, we cannot do that.
Neither am I surprised when the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings comes to my rescue. He does that for two reasons: first, he is a Nova Scotian, something that goes deeper than politics; secondly, twenty years ago we did a lot of work together trying to untangle the economic bear traps in which veterans were being caught. We have a good deal in common.
I shall not detain the house long, but I have risen this evening to try to straighten the record a bit, because I think it was badly tangled this afternoon by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair). I know the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the hon. member for Coast-Capilano want to keep the record straight. This is not the time, in my opinion, to tangle it up needlessly. It is tangled badly enough as it is, but when we see a deliberate attempt to put another twist in it, then I think that is unpardonable. First I would straighten out the hon. member in
The Budget-Mr. Gillis his criticism of the speech made this afternoon by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart). I thought the criticism was quite uncalled for, because I felt the hon. member for Winnipeg North was trying to be helpful. In this party we have no experts, no financial critics as such. Most of the members of this group graduated from the school of hard knocks. But the party itself is a logical protest against the inactivity of the old political parties-because if they were doing a good job there would be no necessity for our being here. The fact that we are here is proof-positive that a large section of the Canadian people are not satisfied.
I would have been quite prepared to let stand the analysis of the budget made this afternoon by the hon. member for Winnipeg North. I have no desire to go further with it because I think on careful examination of the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) it will be found that in his analysis of the picture as it is now and as it may be in the future he has given the house a lot of thought-provoking information. But, as I said, my main purpose in getting up this evening was to straighten the record.
I do not think the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) did himself justice this afternoon. He told us that he had gone to the library to dig carefully into the history of excess profits taxes, and had come to the conclusion that there was no room or need for it in this country. He based his argument upon a statement made by Hugh Dalton some three years ago when he was chancellor of the exchequer in the British government.
The hon. member did not dig back very far. I suppose he found what he was looking for but when you look hard enough for a thing you are apt to find it regardless of whether it is right or wrong. I was reminded of a story my mother used to recite when I was a small boy. Two men were in jail together in the same cell. When the one looked through the prison bars he saw mud, but when the other looked through he saw stars. It depends on what you are looking for. I think the hon. member for Coast-Capilano was in that position this afternoon when he was in the library. If he had wanted to seek for the truth in his examination of the record it was there to be found. But regardless of the merits or demerits of the present situation he was simply looking for something to use in a political way against the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart), who I think tried to do an honest job. In order to put the record straight I am going to quote from an analysis to show whether there is room in Great Britain for an excess profits tax and whether there is

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is the federal tax only.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The over-all picture in Canada as far as the federal government is concerned is a tax of 35 per cent on corporate profits as against 55 per cent in Great Britain. In my opinion there is a lot of room for some kind of tax on Canadian corporate profits. I merely wanted to set the record straight on that point because of what had been said by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, who is the minister's assistant. I believe the minister wants to be fair. I do not think the hon. member did himself justice when he got up and tried to prove to the house that we were crazy, irrelevant and all that kind of thing when we suggested that there was room for an excess profits tax in Canada in order to help hold down inflation.
The next point in connection with straightening the record has reference to the imjfosition of price control. I think the record is a bit tangled up in this connection. Some think that there is no necessity for it now. The Minister of Trade and Commerce


tMr. Howe) has asked for stand-by legislation which can be put into operation at any time conditions in the country warrant. He may not have to use those powers for some considerable time.
I think the field in which there is the greatest emergency is the field of runaway prices. I doubt if there is a more disturbing factor in the country. Reference was made this evening to the railroad strike and I shall not refer further to it because it is partially settled and I hope it will not be resurrected. I think the underlying factor of that strike was the runaway prices together with the fact that no attempt was made to deal with them. There were prolonged negotiations but I am pretty sure that the men who took that step did it as a gesture to bring attention to the seriousness of the uncontrolled cost of living.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No doubt about that.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister has stated
emphatically that it is not intended to impose price control. What would have been wrong with the Minister of Finance taking the same step as that taken by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and asking for stand-by legislation which could be imposed if people did not keep their prices in line? If we had the machinery it could be put into operation overnight. But the minister has no stand-by legislation and he is powerless to do anything about inflation in the country without invoking the War Measures Act. I submit that he should have taken the precaution of enacting stand-by legislation.
Let us look at what happened to the cost of living in the United Kingdom as compared with Canada between June, 1945, and June, 1950. The official figures are as follows: Taking the index for the United Kingdom at 100 for June, 1945, it went from 100 to 114 in June, 1950. Taking the Canadian index for the same period, in June, 1945, it was 119.5, and by June, 1950, it had gone up to 165.4. The increase in Great Britain was 14 points or 14 per cent. The increase in Canada of 45.9 equals 38 per cent. There is a terrific difference there. They have price control machinery in Great Britain, and they also have wage control machinery. There is no doubt that in that country there is pressure for wage adjustments, but Great Britain has had many more difficulties to contend with than we have had. They have had to dig themselves out of the rubble of the last war. Nevertheless the figures I have just given show that, by using the control machinery they had in force during the war, they have equalized the problems, spread them over the

general public as a whole, and succeeded in holding down the cost of living. The figures surely indicate that they have been successful in holding prices within reason and at the same time enacting an excess profits tax as another measure for holding down inflation.
I know that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is a much better economist than I am, and knows the mechanics of finance much better than I do. If he puts the amount of money we have appropriated for defence purposes into circulation, and at the same time converts 25 per cent of our plants, let us say, to war production, thus curtailing the production of consumer goods to that extent, the only thing that can happen will be that prices will be shoved up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If we have that much you will have a lot higher taxes than you have now.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I believe the minister should at least have stand-by legislation so that he may clamp it on if the necessity warrants. If it does not, if everybody is good, if everybody recognizes the problem and tries to hold prices within reason, then he will not have to use it. There is another point I should like to make before I finish. I think the hope of the world of the future depends on the United Nations. I visualized-and I think almost everyone did who took part in the setting up of the United Nations-that some time in the future it would be the nucleus for world government. I think everybody also recognizes that the world has shrunk to the point where that will be necessary in the future. While we pay a great deal of lip service to the United Nations and what they are doing, we do not accept our commitments to that organization very realistically. We do not do much about them. For example, there is a report entitled "National and International Measures for Full Employment" by a group of experts of the United Nations. It deals with the whole question of raising living standards and what should be done. If you will look at the bottom of page 64 and the top of page 65, you will find that this committee of experts of the United Nations decided that one of the most essential things in the world today to maintain full employment, raise standards of living and prevent aggression and the rise of communism, was for each country to enter into a long-term investment program in the backward countries. They set that out very clearly as something that must be done.
The situation in Canada, the United States and every one of these countries today is merely a symptom of the disease. You do not cure a disease by treating the symptoms. That is exactly what we did in the last war, and we seem to be headed in the direction of war again. You have to get at the 69262-42
The Budget-Mr. Gillis disease itself, and the disease is malnutrition. Millions of people in the world have not enough to eat. They are much worse off today than they were when the last war took place because most of those countries had some kind of production, some kind of standard of living. Today they have been devastated, smashed and torn to pieces. They are filled with maimed children and people with broken minds. There is not much to work with. If there is any hope for peace and sanity in the world of the future, I think it has to come from the North American continent. As I pointed out in the house before, we have only 7 per cent of the population of the world and we are producing 45 per cent of the production of the world. I believe the potential figures are about 57 per cent of the world's productive capacity, and some time in the future about 10 per cent of the population. Then again I do not think you can sell the people of Canada and the United States the idea that they should give stuff away. Everybody gets their back up at that suggestion and says that they have to pay taxes. If you can make it an investment that will pay returns directly to this country in the future, then I think you can sell the idea to the people of Canada and the United States. Then I do not think that the devastated countries want to go on relief. I believe they want loans or investments from this continent, but they want to decide for themselves, with technical assistance from us, what they are going to do with the money, and how they are going to build for the future.
Unless something like that is done, I think we are just going to keep on treating the symptoms and not get at the root cause of the disease. So far as I can ascertain, I think one of the most practical propositions was made by Walter Reuther, president of the United Auto Workers. On behalf of his organization Reuther suggested that the United States should make $13 billion a year available to the United Nations for the next one hundred years. He recommended that they set up an economic commission within the structure of the United Nations to use that money for the purpose of developing backward countries. He pointed out further that such an amount of money seems like a staggering sum, but it is only about one per cent of the total amount spent by the United States on the last war, and nothing was solved. If the United Nations is going to be the kind of body that we hope it will be in the future, it must have something to work with, and you must have some honesty among the people who carry on that administration.
Just a couple of weeks ago the British Labour party also made a similar proposal for a global assistance plan. It was pretty much

The Budget-Mr. Gillis along the lines of Reuther's proposition, but they do not spell out in terms of dollars the amount that they figure should be put into the United Nations. They have made that gesture. The British Labour party recognizes that something like that must be done. I think it would not be a bad idea for the Secretary of State for External Affairs to bring before the house a concrete figure representing the amount of money that Canada can afford at this time. We cannot afford not to take that kind of action. We will show that we are ready to recognize such assistance as one of the main weapons with which to prevent wars in the future. We would show that we are ready to co-operate with Great Britain in this global assistance plan, that we are willing to examine the proposal of the auto workers, and are willing to abide by the recommendations of our own experts on the United Nations commission; and we are prepared to participate at any time, through machinery set up by the United Nations, in a long-term investment program for the development of the backward countries.
I think something like that has to come if we do not want to continue on the road we are following now, and perhaps bring about another mess such as we had the last time. Now we have the United Nations to work through, and I believe we should work through that agency. In spite of the obstruction of Russia since its formation, I believe the United Nations has done a good job. You can imagine what the tension would be in the world today, disorganized, messed up and mixed up as it is, if we did not have a body like the United Nations at least trying to iron out these difficulties at that level.
Then I want to say that while the Marshall plan was a good stopgap move which provided a great deal of assistance, at the same time it was actually relief. I have heard some very strong criticism by some of the countries to which Marshall aid was given to the effect that the administrative machinery was not good, that very little aid actually seeped through to the man in the street who was starving and half clothed. That period is over, but through the Marshall plan and UNRRA I believe we have gained sufficient experience at the international level to be able to set up machinery within the United Nations not only to prepare to make money and goods available but also to send in technicians who would help develop these countries from the grass roots along democratic lines.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would the hon. member permit one question? I assure him I am asking it merely for information. According to the scheme he has enunciated and having regard to population, the cost to Canada


would be $1,300 million per year for this period of years. What would be the difference between providing that amount of money in this way and the moneys provided under the Marshall plan? What different treatment would be given it?

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The difference is that there is a limit to Marshall aid; within a year or so it will end completely. What I am talking about now, what Walter Reuther is talking about and what the British Labour party is talking about, is a global plan to replace Marshall aid once it ends. As I said before, Marshall aid was relief; it was given away. I think the time has come when through the United Nations and supervised by the United Nations the countries within that organization should make funds available, on a per capita basis, to the backward countries where communism is flourishing and will continue to flourish unless we get in there and do something for them. By investing in such countries they become tied up with us. We have trained personnel we can lend; and if it is honestly carried through in my opinion it would bring about the sort of thing many people are discussing. I refer to all the talk we hear about one world, the brotherhood of man, help thy neighbour, and all that kind of stuff. Unless we get around to that we will just continue as we are now, and we are not getting anywhere. We fight a war; we think it is all over, but the shooting has never stopped since 1939. It is still going on, and in my opinion it is only by machinery of this kind at the international level that we can hope to cure the ills from which we suffer.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not quarrelling with the hon. member; I am inclined to agree with him, but I am just trying to find out the difference in treatment between this $1,300 million and the billions spent under the Marshall plan.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I thought I had explained that a moment ago. I really do not want to go into the mechanics of the Marshall plan, because a fellow might say a lot of things he would not want to say about it. The Marshall plan and UNRRA were brand new experiences. That is what we are up against today in all the mechanics of society. I have said before in this house that in 1939 we closed the old book. There is no history to guide us through this period. We are tackling the problem of developing world organizations. It is no longer an internal problem; it is the external pressures on this country that are disturbing us so greatly. We may make mistakes. Many mistakes were made under the Marshall plan; nevertheless all these

efforts give us some guide tor the future. The United Nations has something to work with, and in my opinion it is a good organization. But it requires funds and personnel.
To realize that we have only to think about Korea. The United Nations had the responsibility of stopping aggression, but when they were definitely up against aggression they did not have much to work with. This report indicates that those who prepared it have thought the problem through. They have decided on certain mechanics, but the fifty-nine members of the United Nations will have to make the wherewithal available to the organizations they have set up and departmentalized to do the kind of job they visualize as having to be done under that charter. Unless we make funds available to be invested through them in the backward countries the United Nations will not be able to perform the function it can perform. In my opinion it is only through that body that we can hope to relieve the tensions and calm the disturbances outside this country that are causing the unrest and trouble from which we are suffering.
I merely rose to say these things because I thought it was time someone began to think about them. I do not know all about them. The Department of Finance and other departments of the government have experts. If by voicing these opinions in the house, opinions gained by reading the statements of others who specialize in these matters, we can cause these experts to think and prepare legislation to be brought into this house along the lines we have suggested, perhaps not in these exact terms but steps in this direction, I think we will be fulfilling our duty in this house.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I can truthfully say I have not taken up too much of the time of the house this session, so perhaps I may be permitted to speak for five minutes this evening, to express through you to the minister my disagreement with some features of this budget.
In the first place, Mr. Speaker, I most emphatically disagree with the tax on pop and chocolate bars. I understand this tax is expected to bring in some $18 million. I also believe that if you put a tax of 50 per cent on the fifty million pounds of axle grease that is sold under the name of margarine, you would realize the same amount of money. I should like to hear from any rural member from Ontario or Quebec who would disagree with that suggestion. Put the tax on at the source. There are only five grease companies that have a monopoly in this business of 69202-421
The Budget-Mr. Cruickshank importing oils, fish offal and so on in order to produce this substitute for pure butter. Let the government put a tax on that, instead of taxing the children of Canada.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
How about the tax on
whisky?

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am all in favour of it. I do not hesitate to say I buy a little myself, even though Hansard is listening; but any man who can afford to buy it can afford to pay any tax, whatever it is, or he should not buy it at all. I am going to be very brief; I am not going to be like the Toronto member who spoke three times, for forty minutes each time, in the most boring tone, the most monotonous voice and the most useless manner. He spoke three times. I am going to take only about five minutes. There is one thing I want to suggest to you, Mr. Speaker. I have suggested my objection to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), and I know he is not going to pay a great deal of attention to what I say. Nevertheless he will live to regret, having regard to his Quebec rural constituents, the fact that he is putting 500 dairy farmers out of action by allowing five grease companies a monopoly in the manufacture of this so-called substitute for butter. The Ontario members from rural ridings will also remember that.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) is not here, but there is one thing I should like to suggest. In my riding there happens to be what I believe is the finest army camp in the Dominion of Canada and, I believe, one of the finest on the North American continent. I believe we can get a greater enlistment in our armed forces -and I am speaking of the regular armed forces-by increasing the accommodation for the married men. Even though I am sorry to see a few around here who have not seen the light, it is the ambition of most men to get married, particularly if they want to serve in the armed forces. At Chilliwack within this last year we built about 165 houses, I believe, or in that neighbourhood. I believe that number should be doubled.
Through you, Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to say this to the Minister of Finance because, after all, the Minister of National Defence has nothing to do with it; it is the treasury board which has the say. The rentals are far too high. I believe you would increase your enlistment tomorrow in the regular Canadian army of these young men who are married or who desire to get married if you cut the ridiculous rentals you have by 50 per cent tomorrow. After all, the government of Canada are not in the business of renting houses in order to make money; or, if they are, they should not be. We are not in that

The Budget-Mr. Cruickshank line of business. I would suggest to the Minister of Finance that these rentals to these married men be cut 50 per cent as of tomorrow.
I do not read these 40-minute speeches from notes every day as does one of the members from Toronto. But in today's Ottawa Journal, I find this headline:
War widow and six children eke living from $31 monthly.
That sort of report is not particularly conducive to enlistment in the Canadian army or in any other army. I am presuming that the press report is correct. When we can talk about the millions and billions that we have to expend on other matters-some of it spent in my own riding and which I am pleased to have spent there-we have nothing in Canada to be proud of when a war widow and six children eke out a living from $31 monthly.
I do not want to take up any more of the time of the house, Mr. Speaker. I entirely disagree with the budget with regard to the tax on soft drinks and chocolate bars. I think the minister knows exactly where I stand on that matter. On behalf of a riding that I happen to represent, I particularly do not agree with that taxation.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Which one is that?

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I seldom mention the name of Fraser Valley in this house. But when you sell at $87 a thousand No. 3 common lumber that you cannot pick up in your hand -and there are a few hon. members within this house who know something about lumber, as I do-and with No. 1 common at $106 a thousand, and that is exactly what it sold for in British Columbia today, and we produce over 50 per cent of the lumber produced in the Dominion of Canada, then when I am told that we have to tax the kiddies' pop bottles or the kiddies' chocolate bars to the extent of an extra cent in order to raise $18 million; when 50 million pounds of axle grease are produced in the Dominion of Canada this year in competition with 500 dairy farmers; and when No. 1 common lumber is sold at $106 a thousand: I cannot agree with that budget, I am sorry to say. I think that the young minister and his young parliamentary assistant have done a marvellous job. There has been some criticism tonight of my colleague the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair). I am not worried about that because the hon. member for Coast-Capilano is capable at any time of taking care of himself in debate with any member of this house on either side. I want to be emphatic in saying through you, Mr. Speaker, that I think the government or the minister made a tremendous mistake in this stupid and useless

tax when they are allowing this axle grease to compete with the dairy farmers and to wipe them out of business in Canada, and when they are allowing No. 1 common lumber to be sold at $106 a thousand without an excess profits tax on it. I did say on a previous occasion, Mr. Speaker, I have never read, nor will I read, a speech.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. F. Higgins (St. John's East):
maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the last time I had the honour of joining in a debate in which the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) was engaged was one which he himself described as the pipe lines filibuster. This is no filibuster in any way, I can assure you, Mr. Speaker. I am quite certain that most hon. members feel that the job has been done here and that it is time for us to finish the speeches and go home. I believe that has been the general feeling. But, Mr. Speaker, do hon. members really agree with that situation when we see the news as outlined in tonight's Journal, when we read the news containing the speech of Right Hon. Winston Churchill as contained in a Reuters dispatch of this evening in the Journal, and as further outlined in the Canadian Press dispatch which has not yet been published? For the benefit of hon. members who felt, as I must confess I did, that it was time to go home, that all the work we had been brought here for had been finished or practically finished and that we could book our passages on Thursday quite happily, I ask this question: In the light of this item in tonight's newspaper, are they prepared to change their views in any way? I do not intend to read the entire article by any means, but this is the dispatch in the Ottawa Journal, from Reuters news agency, dated London, September 12:
Winston Churchill appealed in parliament today for "a European army of at least 60 to 70 divisions" to make "some sort of front in Europe." He was speaking in the debate on Britain's new three-year rearmament drive . . . "our approval is not a vote of confidence in the government-least of all on its handling of military affairs."
"We have to form as fast as possible a European army of at least 60 to 70 divisions to make some sort of front in Europe and to close what I have called the hideous gap in the protection of western Europe from the Russian communist onrush to the sea," he said.
Churchill suggested that three divisions in Germany and one and a half or two available in Britain did not seem to be a proportionate contribution on Britain's part, even allowing for the fact that she still had important overseas obligations.
"If an army of 60 to 70 divisions can be deployed on our gaping eastern front, the greatest threat of world war in the next three or four years will be substantially diminished if not indeed removed," Churchill said.
"This will undoubtedly give the western democracies the best chance of securing a return in the normal relationships of states and nations. Whether we shall have time or not no one can tell."

Those are the remarks from Mr. Churchill, according to a Reuters dispatch, Mr. Speaker.
I saw a copy of the Canadian Press dispatch which said that he called for two or three divisions from Canada for Europe. In view of that, Mr. Speaker, and in view of the other statements that appeared in this evening's Journal such as "Europe may hold house", hon. members should be told what the situation is. Let me quote further from the Journal:
Members of parliament, who expected to get away from the capital some time this week, may well be held here to deal with legislation necessary to give effect to the sending of arms and men to Europe, a source close to the cabinet said today.
Older parliamentarians have told me that that may be a reporter talking to himself, but I have no knowledge of that. The report continues:
Washington reports have indicated the United States will ask Canada for probably one division to bolster western union defences in Europe.
While no formal request has been made as yet it is expected to come at the meeting of foreign ministers to be held Friday and Saturday.
If that is a clear exposition of the facts, Mr. Speaker, and if there is likelihood of a request being made on Friday or Saturday, then I for one have no hesitation in saying tonight that in so far as being delayed is concerned, we should be delayed. I feel that parliament should not adjourn until some definite decision has been made, if a request of this kind is to be made, because we have not yet had any plans whatsoever for the enlisting of manpower, other than the taking care of what the government calls the Korean episode. No plans are envisaged for a general manpower mobilization of any kind. In view of the stirring remarks of Mr. Churchill, and in view of the request that may be made this week, it is going to be very difficult for hon. members to reconcile themselves to the fact that they will be satisfied to go home at the end of the week.
I merely make those remarks; it is up to parliament. I have no say whatsoever in the matter, nor would I want to have any say in it. We should have a statement on the matter from somebody who is in the know as to whether or not this request is to be made, and whether it is likely or not that Canada will be asked to recruit three divisions to go into the field. It does appear improper, to say the least, that hon. members should not know the situation and should not be given advice as to what is to be done. I believe the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) must indicate what is to be done. I have read, and I have heard him say, that in such an event parliament would make the decision,
The Budget-Mr. Higgins and that would mean the recall of parliament. It would appear to me to be a ridiculous situation to adjourn one day and be recalled a matter of three or four days hence.
I submit that we should stay in session until this particular request, which is likely to be made, is answered one way or the other.
That may not be the view of all hon. members. In fact they may not agree with me at all on it. I am quite certain that in so far as this particular budget is concerned the view of most hon. members is not expressed at all. I feel that deep down in their hearts they were very glad that the demands were as little as they were, but the reason for that is obvious. It was a selfish and personal one, namely, that the individual would not have to meet any worth-while increased taxation. But, Mr. Speaker, if we are honest with ourselves in this matter, if we really want to be honest, and say what we think about this budget, the only thing we can say has been said. I am not making any remarks that have not been made in this house before. I am sure it is merely a pop bottle budget, if you like. It is nothing more or less than that. It is a bit of soothing syrup for the people of Canada.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), in his wisdom-and I do not decry his wisdom; far be it from me to do sudh a thing-may feel that it is quite ample for the purpose; but is that a fair position to take? Is it a fair position to put to the people of this country today, in view of the situation that we are facing? I do not care what the government of this country says. You have heard it from this side of the house right through this debate and through the days of this session. This is by far the gravest emergency that this country has ever faced in its history.
I am no wizard, financially or otherwise. There are only two ways of making more money: one is by earning more and the other is by saving more. I think it is an admitted fact that we must have more money to meet our commitments. We are merely skimming by to get the money that we have to get, and which this budget calls for. We are merely skimming by on our commitments. We are not living up to what we think we are as a nation. We are not doing any more than we should if we were merely a little colony.
If the Korean war is merely one episode in the life of this nation today, then we have to meet our commitments to our partners in the Atlantic pact, and we have to meet our commitments to our partners in the United Nations. I repeat, with very little knowledge of finance, but having listened carefully in the house and having read what I had not listened to, we have not the money

The Budget-Mr. Higgins in this country today in government pockets to meet the commitments that we have. There are two ways to obtain it. The first is by increasing taxation. And, Mr. Speaker, much as we may like the budget as it is, we cannot help saying that it has been tempered very definitely to the political winds.
Do not let us fool ourselves in this matter. Too many responsible ministers of the crown have told us what our danger is. We have too many warnings as to the intentions of the people on the other side of the world in the U.S.S.R. Nobody denies the fact that Russia's intention is to dominate the world by hook or by crook. There is no question whatsoever in anybody's mind as to that fact. What is holding back Russian domination? Chiefly it is the western world powers. The only contribution that Canada can make in the way of real help is by increasing her armaments in every way possible, and by increasing her manpower to the limit that she can.
I have heard many criticisms of the remarks made by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). I am not making any comment one way or the other but I would suggest that hon. members come back to the House of Commons six or seven months from now and ask themselves this question: Was the hon. member for Kamloops right, or was he wrong?
I say this budget has been much too small. What should be done about it? As I said earlier, we have been fed this soothing syrup in the budget to too great an extent altogether for the people in the country to realize the situation. What is needed is a jolt, a real jolt in thq arm by way of greatly increased taxation. Otherwise, if we are not going to have that increased taxation our people are being permitted to go through a period of *twilight sleep in this twilight of peace.
We will have to face an increased budget next year; there is no question about that at all. Why could we not have had some increase at this time? Why could we not have been prepared now for the great difference between this time and what we may expect next March?

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is a by-election coming off.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member may be right. I do not yet know enough about the political game in Canada to be able to say whether that is so or not. But surely the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the cabinet would not be influenced by a by-election! I could not believe that possible-coming from an honest little province like Newfoundland. It is hard to realize that things like that could happen in the world, although I suppose they could.


Be that as it may, I suppose the longer we live the more we learn. It is my honest view that, in so far as increased taxation is concerned, in the words of the old expression we used to have in Newfoundland: Force put when the devil drives. The devil is certainly driving in this case, and we have got to do something about it. There is no one in this country today so blind as to fail to realize the amount of money being spent on luxuries. None of us is so blind as not to realize what these luxuries mean by way of making the people of our country soft. I do not mean that they become foolish, but they want to follow a soft way of living. That soft way of living may be very quickly changed if by any chance-and it is not impossible-a country like Russia were dominating Canada. Our whole way of life would change immeasurably if such a thing were to happen.
With all due respect to the government and its supporters, that is why I am afraid that, while the budget was welcome, it does not reflect the situation we have before us. It does not face up to the situation we have to meet today. There can be no question about that in any way. I say, and I believe it has been said before, that the only way we can avert what is in store for us is by making preparations now, before it is too late.
There can be no question, to use a trite expression, that it is later than you think. I think it is later than most of us think in this western democracy of ours-very much later than you think. The only solution is to do all we possibly can to get as well prepared as we can in the time we have left.
Members of the official opposition and of the other two opposition parties have been criticizing, and properly so, expenditures in the past for defence. I do not think there is any doubt that current and future expenditures for defence will receive the support of the House of Commons. The real cause for complaint however from members of this party and, I believe, the other two parties, has been that there is too much waste, and that non-essential expenditures are constantly taking place. I would refer particularly to the amendment of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) in this connection.
Hon. members are fully aware of one way of making money, and that is by economizing. The same principle applies to government administration. I am entirely in accord with the proposal to cut back public works projects which are not necessary for defence or not productive of any wealth for the country. It is in this connection, and using the phraseology which, I admit, I read in the newspaper today, that I introduce two more points which I feel should be brought to the attention of the house.

Thus far the debate has been kept at a high level and, with the exception of the remarks concerning apples a short time ago, nothing of a provincial nature has been discussed. I have in mind two subjects which, although provincial in their nature, because of the defence situation and the necessary expenditures in that regard, I feel should be brought to the attention of the house.
Since I have been a member I have drawn to the attention of the minister concerned the necessity for the lengthening of the runways at Gander. On each occasion neither the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) nor the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Clax-ton) seemed to think there was any necessity for any action. It was only yesterday that I received an answer to my question in connection with lengthening the runways at Gander airport. These inquiries have been going on since last November. As reported at page 529 of Hansard, my questions were:
1.	Have any arrangements been made to lengthen the runways at Gander airport?
2.	If so, by how many feet, and when is the work to begin?
The answer by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) is as follows:
Plans and specifications are being prepared for the lengthening of one runway to 8,600 feet, with a bearing capacity of 150,000 pounds. It is expected the work will get under way as soon as weather permits in the spring of 1951.
I cannot believe the minister is serious in that answer, when he says there will be only one runway lengthened, and that the work will not begin until next spring. That is a most extraordinary statement in view of the necessity for defence measures at the Gander airport. One runway is not sufficient; there should be at least two cross runways to take care of wind changes-because, like the changes of wind in this honourable chamber, we also have changes of wind at Gander.
What brought the matter particularly to my attention tonight was an article appearing in that great newspaper, the Ottawa Journal, stating:
Handle Biggest Aircraft Vast Airfield On Par With Dorval
Notice has been filed with the Ottawa registry office for expropriation of 3,800 acres-about six square miles of land-south and east of the present Uplands airport.
The expropriation will expand the airport to ten times its present size and make it one of Canada's largest.
It will be on a par with Dorval, Goose and Gander, and will be able to handle the biggest aircraft now flying.
And then further down:
One of the key proposals is the lengthening and strengthening the runways at Uplands to allow accommodation of the largest planes now in operation.
The Budget-Mr. Higgins
These include the giant DC-6, the Boeing Strato-cruiser, and planes of the North Star and Constellation type which are too large for scheduled landings on the existing air strips there.
It says that the cost is to be $5 million. There is quite an extensive plan accompanying the article and in the description it states that the new airport will be ten times the size of the present airport and will accommodate a fighter squadron for the protection of the capital. I am a newcomer to this house and to Ottawa; I appreciate the importance of Ottawa and I know it is a lovely city, but is there any necessity of having the airport at Uplands increased to this extent while an airport so vital to defence as Gander is to have only one runway extended, and that not to be done until 1951? If that makes sense then maybe I am as crazy as most people think I am, but I cannot see it. That is just another example of unnecessary expenditure of government funds.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Liberal management.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It may be Liberal in the sense of being made by a Liberal government, but it certainly is not liberal in extent. I am glad the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) is in his seat because there is a matter I want to bring to his attention. This also relates to expenditures that should be made for defence purposes. As the minister knows, and as many hon. members know, at Wabana, Bell island, we have the largest iron mine in the British empire. This mine has been in operation for fifty years and has turned out a tremendous tonnage of iron ore. It is still continuing to turn out a great tonnage. This fact has been brought to the attention of the house on previous occasions, but it is in connection with our present defence measures that I am bringing it again to the attention of hon. members.
I have asked repeatedly that the pier which provides the only connection between Bell island and the mainland should be repaired. On June 16 last I outlined the reasons why repairs should be made and the Minister of Public Works said that they would be done. But nothing has been done. In August Premier Smallwood of Newfoundland made a statement to the press and blamed the resident engineer of the department for the work not having been done. He said that that engineer should be removed because he was simply a hindrance to work being done. The minister was away and I do not blame him for this but I feel sure that there were at least one or two assistants in his department. I hold no brief for Mr. Miller, but I must say that I have found him most co-operative and interested in his work in Newfoundland. I think the accusation was unnecessary and uncalled for.

The Budget-Mr. Higgins
Yesterday I obtained an answer to a question I had asked, which was somewhat similar to the one I had asked on June 16 when the minister said that repairs would be made. I had asked what steps were being taken with respect to repairs to the wharf at Portugal cove. The minister's reply, to be found on page 530 of Hansard, was as follows:
No steps are being taken by this department for repairs to this wharf. It serves as a wharf for the ferry plying to Bell island, which is entirely within the province of Newfoundland, and the dominion government does not accept responsibility for the upkeep of such ferry wharves.
Will the dominion government accept responsibility if there is a bogging down in the production of iron ore? Or is that to be the responsibility of the provincial government? Is it going to be the responsibility of the Minister of Public .Works or of the poor unfortunate Mr. Miller who has been blamed for a lot of things? I make no apology for bringing before this house a matter which may be considered provincial in character during a debate which has been on so high a level.
In my opinion these matters are vital to the defence scheme for this country. Definite steps should be taken with respect to Gander airport and the wharf at Portugal cove, which is vital to the existence of ten thousand people on the island who are now producing iron ore for defence purposes. The excuse that this is a. wharf for a provincial ferry is not enough. The ferry may hold water, but the excuse certainly does not.
It may be right to say that public provincial ferries do not come under dominion jurisdiction but the two little boats that ply between Bell island and Portugal cove would not fit that description. I ask the minister to reconsider this matter and see if he cannot do something for the Portugal cove wharf.

I do not think it hurts anybody to be told the truth that there is a real emergency in


Canada. From my knowledge of the Canadian people, which perhaps is a bit new although I have not been befogged by being in the woods too long, I know that if they are told the facts they are prepared to stick with those facts and do their utmost to help this country make a real contribution to the British commonwealth of nations, to our partners in the United Nations and to the countries of the North Atlantic pact.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is again my misfortune to be the last speaker this evening, when hon. members are desirous of seeing the debate come to an end. That does not deter me from saying what I intend to say so long as I can get anyone, including yourself, to listen to me indulgently.
I am not going to say very much in commendation of the minister's budget speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I shall stay anyway.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Therefore I may appear to be somewhat at variance with a good many hon. members. Before commencing to say what I feel I should say i should like to echo the remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) who indicated that he felt like getting down on his knees to thank the Lord that there was not a Conservative government in power today endeavouring to fight a war according to Conservative principles. Every one of those hon. gentlemen, including the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, has got up to tell the house that what we need to do is to tighten our belts and have more restrictions in the country. 1 would imagine that, as it is already, probably eighty per cent of the people in Canada today are under the gravest anxiety as to how they are going to finance their domestic affairs during the next year. I do not think there is a doubt about that. If hon. members will be quite frank with the people of their constituencies when they go home, I think hon. members will soon discover, when they start talking to them, how they feel about paying the exorbitant prices they are paying for coal and many many other things which they have to buy. They will discover how they feel about the extortionate rents they are paying, and the almost inconceivable amount of money that it costs to build a house nowadays in a land where I imagine housing material is produced as abundantly as it can be produced in any nation on the face of the earth.
These are just two or three of the little things. For a man to rise as the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) has done, and as other members have done, and tell us

that we should tax our people more and that we should have deflation in the face of that sort of situation, is almost to insult the intelligence of the Canadian people and strike despair and dismay into their hearts. It is so tragically, fantastically and utterly unreal. That is the point. Shortly I am going to quote some passages from the excellent speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) the other day to show how unreal it is that Canada at the present time should have anything like deflation, tightening belts, scarcity, austerity, which seem to obsess the minds of the hon. gentlemen among the Progressive Conservatives.
Their leader did not say anything specific about this matter. He does a lot of beautiful talking, but I find it very hard to pin him right down to a definite commitment on any particular item in Canadian public life. It may be that I am not skilled in interpreting his language, but that is how it is. I regard the Conservatives with every kind of respect.
I understand the Conservative attitude.' It is exactly the attitude that our grandfathers had. But what a difference between the world of today and the world in which our grandfathers carved their homes out of the forests. With none of the machines, technological skills, modern appliances and the advantages which we possess today, it was utterly necessary for them to be scarcity minded at every turn of the way, and to be severely economical.
It is the inability of a great number of people of our time to realize the necessary impact on the civilization in which we live of the discovery and employment of machines, solar power and technological skills that has put this nation, together with so many nations of the world, in such grave danger as now threatens it.
Therefore I say quite frankly, with the very best of good feeling toward the minister, that as an orthodox scarcity-mentality budget speech there is little to find fault with in his speech and much to commend but as an age-of-abundance budget speech there is plenty to find fault with and very little to commend.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Louder.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You do not realize what you are asking for down there.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Give it to them.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Here is a general statement which I commend to the members of the house with the utmost solemnity: The policies of the minister cannot possibly render financially possible what is physically possible in this nation. I would imagine. that
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore every member of every party would say in general terms that what is physically possible must be financially possible. It was repeated and repeated by the members of the cabinet in world war II, but never once did the cabinet in world war II approach within a short distance of making what was physically possible in Canada financially possible. They judged what was financially possible by the amount of money they could wring out of people through taxes on chocolate bars, ice cream cones, all sorts of little things, and then the big things too. They thought that was what was financially possible. But what was in reality physically or financially possible in Canada we did not once approach in the last war, nor have we yet approached what is actually physically possible.
We shall examine four or five things that exist right in Canada today and see whether the minister does not agree that after all there is something strangely wrong. I recall to the house one fine instance which the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) gave this afternoon. He pointed out that in the Dominion of Canada from 1939 until 1950 somebody or some agencies have created outright $12 billion of money, and the policies of the Liberal government have saddled that $12 billion on the backs of the Canadian people today as a debt. Unless the financial policies of this country change, their children and their children's children forever will be called upon to bear that burden and pay interest thereon.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Will anyone in his saner moments, and within the sound of my voice, tell me that a war that was fought with blood, sweat and tears by virtually every family in this nation was not paid for with blood, sweat and tears? When we took our natural resources, changed them into vast fighting machines and with them overwhelmed the enemy, will anyone tell me that wa>
did not pay for that war? Looking at this matter from the standpoint of the simplest elementary common sense, in addition to paying for the war with the four fearful prices of blood, sweat, tears and natural resources, is it reasonable that we and our children's children be saddled with a $12 billion debt?
Will anyone tell me that it was not physically possible to avoid that in Canada? They did not make what was physically possible in Canada financially possible. Dear me, when the Indians roamed over the plains and hills and among the forests fighting wars they won their wars with blood, sweat, tears
658	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore and the natural resources they found at their disposal, but they owed no debt when they were finished.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They had no ministers of finance in those days.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: With all our intelligence and civilization, with all the machines at our disposal, why should we not be able to do as well as the savages did?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There was no Indian branch then either.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let us face that fact as responsible members of parliament in this most portentous hour. There seems to be plenty of levity, but we have had too much levity for twenty years. It is time now to cut out the levity and get right down to common sense. When we find a question we cannot answer, let us not try to laugh it off. It is not a laughing matter, and it is not going to be a laughing matter in the years to come. With another $12 billion or $20 billion added to the debt of this nation in the next five years, where shall we be? The policies of the Minister of Finance will put this nation into debt to the extent of $20 billion exactly as the same policies in the hands of Mr. Ilsley put the nation into debt to the extent of $12 billion. That was to fight a war, for which we had already paid. I think hon. members will agree that in a general sort of way, though I have not set out the technicalities, I have pretty well established my point, that the policies of the minister are not capable of making financially possible what is physically possible in this country. We should have had $12 billion worth of credit in this nation instead of $12 billion of debts. We should have had $12 billion of financial assets, just as we have the billions of dollars' worth of assets in our great industrial plants throughout the nation. They are assets; but this financial handicap which has been hung about our necks renders it almost impossible for us to enjoy the good things that are available as a result of our efforts*
So I say the budget speech by the minister was not a success from the standpoint of an age of abundance and modernization. It would have been bad enough seventy-five years ago; it just is not good enough today. Now, of course, we are going to hear a lot of foolishness about funny money, just as though the dollar with which we fought the last war was not funny.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That was because of what was done by the premier of Alberta.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I know all about what the premier of Alberta did, so you are not telling me anything new.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Then don't be surprised at an interjection like that.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I pick them up whenever I hear them, because they indicate something wrong with the mentality of the person making them; that is all. I sympathize and pity you, and I want to put you right before you make too many mistakes. Let me point out that your own dollar with which you fought the last war has lost more than half its value in ten years. You do not think that is a funny money dollar, do you? In addition to the debts, in addition to the blood, the sweat, the tears and the loss of material resources in the last war, we have our dollar cut by more than fifty per cent of its value.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is sound money.

maintopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And you call that sound
money, as if anything could be funnier than that! That is worth considering; I would recommend that everyone give it very careful thought because we are on the threshold of another colossal financial blunder such as we committed in 1939. That is as obvious as can be.
I want to give an example of just one of the deficiencies of our system. Every hon. member knows the tragic situation prevailing throughout this country in respect of housing. What is the cause of the tremendous increase in the cost of housing? Why is it that today we think in terms of $7,000, $8,000, $9,000 and even $10,000 for a new house when ten years ago we were thinking in terms of $2,500 and $3,000? What is the cause of that? If it is not your financial system, tell me what it is. The raw materials are here; the human resources are here, just as they were ten years ago; and we have machines and skills we did not have then. If this exorbitant increase in the cost of everything pertaining to housing is not the result of the financial system, directly and completely, just figure out what it is the result of; then get up and give a talk on it, and explain to us.
Here is an illustration of the sort of thing that has had to be faced in Canada even since parliament met in this special session. It is the case of a soldier with a splendid record in world war II. He is a young man, a sergeant with a wife, a baby and a three-year old child. He was born in my own city of Lethbridge, and therefore I am particularly interested in his case. Here is his situation: He has been transferred from an air station where he had some kind of a house; and here is a letter written by his wife about September 7. I am going to use the name "Tim" so no one can find out who this boy is; and

instead of giving the name of the city I will say "X". The letter reads:
Tim got an auto camp for us-$5 a day, at city X, and we have been here a week. Nobody wants you with children-it is a heartless situation-and rents are extortionate. Tim found a house, fully furnished, seven miles out of city X-rent is $75 per month.
You do not need any more, do you, than to hear that a sergeant who within a month may give his life for his country, who is trying to raise a family to fight the next horrible war your policies will bring on, cannot find a house when he is transferred, and who finally has to pay $75 a month for a house seven miles from the city, while the defence department pays no attention. You do not want any more than that, do you? Will anyone pretend that such things are physically necessary in Canada? They have
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore been rendered financially necessary by the methods pursued by the Minister of Finance and the Liberal and Conservative parties in this country.
Not only do we find such difficulties confronting our married service personnel. Similar perplexities are facing civilian people from coast to coast in this country right now. Let us not pretend that the people who have been managing this nation financially have known even the elements of what is necessary to rule a country like Canada in an age of abundance. I shall have more to say tomorrow, Mr. Speaker.
On motion of Mr. Blackmore the debate was adjourned.
